speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: TREATMENT OF CANADIAN NATIONALS BY COMMUNIST AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
I should like to make a short statement regarding the treatment of Canadians in China.
The house will wish to know that the United Kingdom charge d'affaires in Peking today presented a note to the Chinese viceminister of foreign affairs on behalf of and with the approval of the governments of Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, regarding the treatment accorded their nationals in China.
The note referred to previous communications on this subject which had expressed grave concern for the widespread arrests and frequent detention incommunicado of foreign nationals, and also drew attention to the hardships suffered by persons who were prevented or delayed from leaving China. The note pointed out that new arrests had taken place and listed the names of fifty-five United Kingdom, Canadian, Australian and United States citizens who are now understood to be in jail. In addition, there is an undetermined number of persons who are understood to be undergoing one form or another of house arrest.
The United Kingdom charge d'affaires has asked the Chinese ministry of foreign affairs for information regarding the charges against those persons who have been arrested, the sentences, if any, which have been passed upon them, and their present whereabouts and welfare. He has also asked for facilities to enable him to communicate with them.
Of the fifty-five, seven Canadians are known to be imprisoned. They are Bishop Cuthbert O'Gara, Bishop Gustave Prevost, Sister Ste. Marie-Germaine, Sister Ste. Alphonse du Redempteur, Sister Raymonde Marie, Father Eugene Lauzon, Father Arsenius Mullin.
Reports received during the past eighteen months from individuals leaving China had indicated that Canadians had not in general been physically maltreated, although some had been subjected to imprisonment and to the humiliation and indignities of what we
would call mock "trials". We are therefore greatly shocked to learn of the death of Father Joseph Leon Arcand at the Franciscan mission hospital at Chefoo on February 8. He had been serving a six months' jail sentence and was brought in a deplorable condition to the hospital where he died shortly after his admission. This is the first case which has come to our attention in which there is reason to believe that the death of a Canadian missionary has been caused or hastened by serious neglect or maltreatment on the part of the Chinese communist authorities.
The fate of the five Sisters of the Immaculate Conception who were tried publicly in Canton on December 2, 1951, has of course been a continuing cause for anxiety. I know all Canadians were relieved to learn that the three sentenced to deportation had reached Hong Kong safely on February 28. However, when we received a first-hand account of their ordeal we were profoundly shocked by the deliberately callous treatment meted out to the sisters, apparently for the purpose of discrediting western humanitarian institutions in China. It seems to be the long-term policy of the Peking government to expel all western missionaries from China, or to make their lives so difficult that they will leave the country. In fact there has been a steady exodus from China of missionaries of all nationalities. According to our information, only 145 Canadians remain in China today, of whom about 100 are missionaries.
I know all hon. members share the concern of the government for the safety and well-being of Canadian missionaries in China and will be glad to be assured that everything within our means will continue to be done to assist them until they can get out.

subtopic: IRREGULARITIES IN ENGINEER DETACHMENT AT PETAWAWA

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: IRREGULARITIES IN ENGINEER DETACHMENT AT PETAWAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the discovery and investigation of grave irregularities in the engineer detachment at Petawawa camp, charges have been laid in the civil court against five civilians and one service officer, and it is expected that further charges will be laid. Mr. J. W. Pickup, Q.C., of Toronto, has been appointed by the Department of Justice as special counsel in these cases.
In view of the rule that a member while speaking must not refer to any matter on which a judicial decision is pending, I shall not refer to that aspect; but hon. members will recognize that this matter has two aspects, one, criminal, with which the courts will deal, and the other, administrative. I am sure the house will permit me to report on the situation and what I am doing to rectify it.
The irregularities first came to the attention of the department several months ago and arose out of the disposal of scrap under contracts made by Crown Assets Disposal Corporation for the sale of thirty tons in 1950 and fifteen tons in 1951.

subtopic: IRREGULARITIES IN ENGINEER DETACHMENT AT PETAWAWA
speechtext: On what date was it first ascertained that there was any trouble?

subtopic: IRREGULARITIES IN ENGINEER DETACHMENT AT PETAWAWA
speechtext:
In October, 1951. An investigation was started immediately, and it was found that under cover of these contracts about 380 additional tons were taken out. Had all the material illegally taken been scrap, it would have had a value of about $9,000, but it included some used shower stalls, stoves, wash sinks ami steel rails. The shower stalls, stoves ana shiks had been salvaged when replaced with new equipment or when old wartime buildings had been taken down. They had not yet been declared surplus pending a further survey to determine which of these items might be useful on a temporary basis. So far as ascertained, the only new material removed was some 600 lengths of soil pipe having a value of about $6 per length. Seizures have been mace or the


material that has been traced, and a considerable part of it should be recovered. It also included a used weighing scale and shovel boom, but these have been recovered.
The investigation has disclosed no foundation for the reports alleging irregularities and deficiencies in the construction of buildings in the twenty-two major construction projects under way at Petawawa. However, other irregularities were found arising out of the employment of engineer civilian and service personnel and equipment, and these are still being investigated by the R.C.M.P. and provost corps. These irregularities also included the sale to contractors of some timber and gravel in the camp area.
It is not possible yet to estimate accurately the loss to the public caused by these irregularities so far discovered, but from the reports so far made it would appear that the total loss to the public may be as much as $50,000. Reports so far indicate that no personnel are involved outside of the engineer detachment at Petawawa and the employees of the civilian contractors.
In addition to the investigation being continued by the R.C.M.P. and the provost corps, I have engaged Mr. George S. Currie, chartered accountant of Montreal, a former deputy minister of national defence, to make a full investigation of the situation, security and accounting procedure for engineer stores, equipment and services at Petawawa and elsewhere; his powers and terms of reference have no restrictions whatever. Everything possible will be done to get to the bottom of this situation and take such action and adopt such remedies as may be required.
In conclusion I would like to add that if in the course of its work the select committee on defence expenditure would like to look into the stockkeeping, accounting or auditing procedure, or any other matter relating to its work, on the spot and anywhere, all facilities will be provided.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO LIABILITY OF DIRECTORS OR OFFICERS OF CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO LIABILITY OF DIRECTORS OR OFFICERS OF CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to strengthen both the Criminal Code and the Combines Investigation Act in preventing monopolistic practices in trade and business by providing for a penalty to be imposed not only on the corporation but also on any director or officer who assents to or acquiesces in such trade practices. As the law now stands, only the corporation is liable for an offence committed under these two acts. This bill would in effect therefore make a director or officer of that corporation guilty of that offence personally and therefore liable, along with the corporation, to penalties as provided under the law.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent for the appointment of a special committee on readjustment of the representation in the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion was called just a few minutes before the house rose for the Easter recess, and I spoke briefly upon it. On looking over the report in Hansard of what I said at that time, I feel that there is not much that I could now add. It would not be proper for me to repeat anything I said then, and I do not think it would be particularly useful to elaborate on it. There is, however, one aspect of the matter about which I should like to take just a few moments of the time of the house, and that is with regard to the form of the resolution on the order paper.
Hon. members will recall that I tried to make it as clear as possible that I was not [Mr Bryce.]

presenting this motion as one on which I would ask those who usually support the government to support my views, but was doing so to provide an opportunity for hon. members to express their own convictions in the light of the responsibility they felt they had the country and to their own constituents with respect to fair representation in the House of Commons. I stated then-and I wish to repeat it-that I tried to draft a motion that would allow all the views that hon. members might entertain on that subject to find expression in this house, but that I was not prepared to put forward a motion that went beyond what I myself would feel it possible for me to support. Therefore I had not presented a motion which would restrict the diminution in representation of any one province to 10 per cent, because that was something which I personally could not support, in view of the fact that it would conserve to Saskatchewan a larger representation than Alberta would obtain, though Saskatchewan at the present time has, according to the last census, a smaller population than Alberta; and also because it would increase the floor of Newfoundland over that of the other maritime provinces; but a restriction in the diminution at any one readjustment of 15 per cent would not have at this time any such undesirable feature.
The motion was drawn for the purpose of restoring to the constitution a provision that was in it originally to temper to some extent the rigidity of the principle of representation by population when there had been rather a small change in the relative population of the provinces. It was felt, though that had been the intention of the one-twentieth provision in the original constitution; that the one-twentieth provision had operated only between two successive censuses, and the consequence had been that there had arisen a disproportion of more than one-twentieth over a period of more than that between two censuses, and that that disproportion was not taken into account. Therefore I tried, in drafting this motion, to make it clear that there would be no such possibility here, and that every time the restriction of 15 per cent applied it would be upon what the representation of the provinces would have been under the rules of section 51 as they stand.
Just to illustrate: under this new principle, if it were adopted, though Saskatchewan would otherwise see its representation reduced by 25 per cent, it would not be reduced by more than 15 per cent. But if there were no change in the situation at the next census, the 15 per cent would apply not to the membership of seventeen that would be saved to Saskatchewan at this time under this rule, but would apply to the membership

of 15 which it would have according to the strict application of the rules in section 51 of the British North America Act. That is the explanation for the language used in this draft resolution:
(a) to provide that the representation of any province in the House of Commons on the readjustment of the representation of the provinces therein on the completion of each decennial census including that for the year 1951 shall not be reduced by more than 15 per cent below the representation to which such province was entitled under rules 1 to 4, inclusive, in subsection (1) of section 51 of the British North America Act . . .
So that if the situation were to remain-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: At the last preceding census.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
At the census that is being considered for the purpose of the readjustment. Under this language, if it is adopted, you would find out what the representation would be, and you would find out what the representation was under rules 1 to 4 of section 51. The last time that was 20 for Saskatchewan. You would apply the 15 per cent to 20, and that would mean that it could be a reduction of three, but not more than three. If there were no change in the trend, and the same situation repeated itself the next time, you would apply the 15 per cent to 15 and not to 17, because 17 would be the number not in accord with the rules, but something saved by the new principle.
Even that might not always overcome the intolerable situation of giving one province with a smaller population a larger representation than another province with a larger population. At the present time Saskatchewan has a larger population than Manitoba, but during the last ten years Manitoba's population increased by 5 [DOT] 8 per cent. If that situation were to continue up to the time of the next census it would mean that the population of Manitoba would be about 45,000 more than it is at the present time-it would be somewhere around 821,000. If there continued, which I think is unlikely, to be a diminution in the population of Saskatchewan -during this decade it was a diminution of 7 [DOT] 5 per cent; even if it were a diminution of only one-third of that, or 2-5 per cent, it would mean that the population of the province would not be equal to Manitoba's 821,000. Nevertheless, by applying the 15 per cent rule to both provinces without any qualification whatever, Manitoba could be reduced from 14 to 12, and Saskatchewan only from 15 to 13, because 15 per cent of their respective representations would bring about that limitation.
Well, in that event the suggestion for the committee to consider is whether it should not provide that Manitoba could not be reduced-if its population were equal to or
Redistribution Committee greater than that of Saskatchewan-below the representation of Saskatchewan.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister permit a question? Was there any representation from the legislature of Saskatchewan that the 10 per cent figure should apply? Has there been any consultation with any of the other provinces in regard to the resolution which was introduced in the legislature by Mr. Tucker, the leader of the opposition in Saskatchewan, and passed unanimously? Has there been any consultation with the other provinces as to the acceptance of the unanimous recommendation of the legislature of Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
As to the first question, representations have been made to the federal government that there was this unanimous resolution passed by the legislature of Saskatchewan. As to the second question, there has been no consultation by the federal government with the other provinces. The hon. member realizes that that is the position this party has always taken-that representation of the people in the House of Commons is not a matter which concerns the governments of the provinces but is a matter which concerns the people of Canada and their representatives in parliament.
The reason for my finding it impossible to put forward the proposal that was made in the legislature of Saskatchewan was that that would result in giving Saskatchewan, with a smaller population, a larger representation than Alberta. The house, of course, is free to do that, if a majority wishes to do it; but I would not be able to support it, and since it is something I cannot support, I cannot put it in the proposal which appears under my name on the order paper.
Personally I do not think this trend is apt to continue; I think the population of Manitoba is apt to increase at a greater rate than 5-8 per cent, which was its increase during the last decade. I think the population of Saskatchewan is going to reverse the trend and that in future it will increase rather than diminish. But, as I say, if this is to be provided as a rule to apply to future readjustments, we should guard against what theoretically could happen, so that if there was the same trend in those two provinces, with the representation of both of them having to be diminished, that of Manitoba could not be diminished below that of Saskatchewan if its population was equal to that of Saskatchewan.
So that there would be two limitations. First there would be the 15 per cent limitation-it could not go beyond that; and, second, it could not go beyond the effect the 15 per cent limitation would have upon a province with the same or smaller population.

Redistribution Committee
It may very well be, as quite a large number of newspapers throughout the country have suggested, that there should be no interference whatsoever with the rules provided in the amendment made in 1946. I would be sorry if that were -the conclusion of a majority in the house, because I think that, whether it be justified or not, there would be resentment among -the people of Saskatchewan at the loss of 25 per cent of their membership in one readjustment. I think it is desirable, in this united nation, that all sections feel that their special situations receive consideration from -the body politic generally, and that we are disposed to take what can be regarded generally as a reasonable attitude in that connection.
This will bring about some small increase in the total representation in the house. First of all there would be an increase of one for the Northwest Territories. That, I think, is something that is apt to be permanent. Indeed, it is possible that the increase by one may, at the time of the next census, be found to be insufficient, because there is development going on in the Northwest Territories, to the advantage of those localities and the advantage of the economy of the nation as a whole.
It will provide Saskatchewan with two more members than it would otherwise be entitled to; but that small increase is not very serious. And, looking over the censuses since confederation, one would feel -that the adoption of a rule like this could not mean a variation of more than -two or three from the 262 now provided by the constitution. This time it would provide for two for Saskatchewan; but I would hope tha-t, next time, the population of Saskatchewan would entitle it to its full membership of 17- perhaps even more than -that. However it could not mean any substantial variation in the total membership of the house. I think it is something which would not be entirely satisfactory to our friends from Saskatchewan, but which will, I hope, make them feel that their fellow Canadians throughout -the whole country sympathize with the fa-ct that [DOT]there has been a diminution in the population, while there has been -a growth in the populations of all other Canadian provinces.
It is worthy of consideration, I think, to remember that -although there has been a-diminution in the number of people counted in Saskatchewan in the last census, there has been no diminution in the contribution of new wealth to the Canadian economy provided by -the people of that province. The diminution results from the fact -that a lesser number of people have been able to carry on agricultural pursuits, and to provide the same return from the soil that was provided before.
[Mr. St. Laurent.l
It is my hope that there will come for Saskatchewan, as there -has come for Alberta, and as there has come for Manitoba, some diversification in their economy which will *make Saskatchewan the home not only of an agricultural population

although that is absolutely essential to the well-being of the country-but the home also of some people whose pursuits will be industrial and commercial, and who will work alongside their fellow Canadians in Saskatchewan who are devoting their energy to the tilling of the soil.
This resolution, of course, does not give -binding directions to the committee to be set up. The house -may decide at this time that it will have no departure whatsoever from the rules at present in the constitution. Under those circumstances the committee would have nothing to do but to determine the limits of each constituency within each province.
If on the other hand the house feels that a certain variation in those rules might well be considered by the committee, then under the terms of the resolution it will allow the committee to give consideration to such modification. I inserted in their resolution the provision that the committee would have the right to call for persons and papers; because if it came to the conclusion that some alleviation should be made, it might want to consider whether it should be done only to meet an exceptional case, in one instance, or whether it should be a new principle which would apply to future redistributions and readjustments.
In that event the committee would want to know how that should be done. It may be the committee would find it expedient to recommend some permanent change in the rules affecting readjustment, and would want to know from the law officers of the crown and the law officers of the House of Commons what would be the correct procedure in order to bring this about. Then it would be for the house to determine whether or not it should be done.
I think there is nothing further I could add that would be of -any assistance in coming to a conclusion. I wish to repeat merely that this is the constitutional responsibility of each one of us, not only of members of the government as members of the House of Commons, but of every other member in the house, -and probably in the same degree as it involves the responsibilities of those who form the present government.
It is not something which can -be determined as an -act of executive government. It is something which must be dealt with by legislation which is the responsibility of -the house, and about which I wish to

make no plea other than to state what my own views are, and to ask each of my fellow members of parliament to make up his mind and to express his views in the light of his own conception of his responsibilities to Canada at large and to his own constituency in particular.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this motion is not only one of very great importance to every member of the house but one of the utmost importance to all Canadians. As the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) emphasized on different occasions during his remarks, the desire of the members of the house at this time should be to provide a system of representation which will meet with satisfaction in every part of Canada and leave the impression not only in every province but in every locality within every province that the system of representation gives as fair an expression of the thoughts and desires of the people of Canada generally as may be devised by the members of parliament at this time. I can only express my regret that, with full knowledge of the fact that this extremely important subject would be coming before the House of Commons for consideration, the government has not seen fit to place before us any new method of dealing with this problem which would give to the people of Canada, as well as to members of parliament who are now called upon to express their opinions, a feeling that we have a system which will stand the test and that it is one which over the years is going to avoid any unfairness or any suggestion that it produces any other result than the most effective representation of our people that can be introduced.
During this session we have heard a speech by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) which I am not at liberty to quote in detail under the rules of the house, but it was a speech which placed before us in clear and cogent terms the necessity for some continuing body to deal with this subject as a continuing process so that at such time as redistribution of the seats of the House of Commons becomes necessary under our constitution the plans for that redistribution will have been laid upon an impartial basis which will be likely to find general acceptance by every member of the house as well as by the people of Canada generally. It would appear that such method of dealing with this essential part of our democratic system is not to be placed before us at this time. Nevertheless the very fact that so many people are thinking about the need for a new 

system, and the very fact that so many Canadians are expressing the hope that there may be nothing savouring of gerrymandering at this or any other time, indicate that in our consideration of this subject, we should be seeking some method which will be satisfactory at least until such time as a new and more satisfactory system is introduced, and that whatever we do we should not deal piecemeal with the problem but should attempt to find a working arrangement that respects our constitution and is in keeping with the very special form of federal system established in this country in 1867.
May I emphasize both personally and on behalf of the members of the Conservative party in this house that we are anxious to see the problem dealt with as quickly as possible. We will support every reasonable measure to deal with the subject expeditiously and justly, not so much for the members of the House of Commons as for the people of Canada whose servants we are. Nevertheless we should not seek any shortcuts which may cause difficulties afterwards, and above all, when we are doing something that is related so directly to the processes of democracy, I submit we should show the utmost respect for that constitution which has settled for us the form of democracy under which we carry on our public affairs.
The resolution now before us calls for the setting up of a select committee and then introduces certain special considerations to be placed before that committee. Although the resolution itself by its wording does not exclude consultation with the provincial governments in dealing with this question, the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) this afternoon left no doubt that his opinion is definitely against such consultation. This is not the first time he has explained his own opinion in regard to consultation of that type. At page 1936 of Hansard for Tuesday, May 28,	1946, the
Prime Minister, who was then minister of justice, in introducing a motion which had as its purpose changing the representation in this house, had this to say:
The provinces, that is to say the people of the provinces, are all represented in this parliament, and for the purposes of such matters as are confided to the jurisdiction of this parliament it is by those representatives here that the people of the provinces speak.
That statement was similar in meaning to the statement by the Prime Minister this afternoon. I do suggest, however, that the question was not settled finally in 1946, and that hon. members should very carefully consider what it is we have before us and whether in fact, with our particular federal system, the provinces as represented by their

own governments have not some interest in the subject at this time. In fact I find it difficult to follow the arguments of the Prime Minister through to their logical conclusion because in effect he is taking into account the representation made by the legislature of Saskatchewan, which representation expressed the unanimous opinion of the members of that body no matter to what party they belonged. Before us in this resolution we have in fact an attempt to meet in part the representation which has been made on behalf of the people of Saskatchewan through the legislature and government of that province. The Prime Minister has explained that he is not prepared to go as far as the resolution of the Saskatchewan legislature went, but he has included in the resolution now being introduced a request that the committee give consideration to the proposal that the number of seats in any province shall not be reduced by more than 15 per cent below the representation to which such province was previously entitled. He has explained why he is prepared to put forward the figure of 15 per cent instead of 10 per cent.
The Prime Minister said he was placing this resolution before the House of Commons with the request that hon. members express their opinions freely and without regarding themselves as bound by the fact that this has been presented by the leader of the government. That is a suggestion with which I am in agreement; in fact I would welcome a wider application of the same suggestion on many other occasions, and I hope this may be a precedent which will be followed in future. I also hope this indicates an increasing belief on the part of the Prime Minister in the effectiveness of committees to deal with matters that require attention, so that in future he will not only be ready to propose other committees but will also suggest on those occasions that whether or not hon. members ordinarily support the government they should regard themselves as completely free to express their opinions as to the way those committees should deal with the matters referred to them. I am not in any way taking issue with the Prime Minister's statement that he brings the resolution before us in this manner when I suggest that a very large number of members of this house have formed the habit of favouring his suggestions when they are placed before us; and for that reason I recognize that when he gives his opinion as to what he would regard as satisfactory, it will at least be given very earnest consideration by those hon. members who ordinarily support him without question.
The Prime Minister indicated, as I understood his words, that he would find it quite
Redistribution Committee satisfactory if the conclusion of the committee should be that the number pf seats should not be reduced by more than 15 per cent below the previous figure. That being so it would seem that the Prime Minister has accepted the principle put forward by the province of Saskatchewan, though he has not been prepared to go quite as far as the legislature of that province went in making this representation. After all, this resolution merely calls upon the committee to consider the proposal. I do suggest that if consideration is to be given to the views of the Saskatchewan legislature, which quite obviously prompted this proposal-and I do not think the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would challenge that-

speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will allow me, the proposal had been discussed and considered even before it came to us in the form of a resolution from the legislature of Saskatchewan. The members in this house representing constituencies in Saskatchewan were quite as much concerned about it as were the members of the legislature, and from the very day they arrived in Ottawa and were informed of the results of the census they suggested that every attempt be made to avoid what they considered would be an unfair action, that is to say a reduction of 25 per cent in their numbers in this house.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will permit me also, the remarks of the Prime Minister relieve me of any further responsibility for answering what has just been stated by the leader of the opposition.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I was not in any doubt but that the right hon. Minister of Agriculture had been making very vigorous representations to the government. In fact I was quite sure that the delay in getting this resolution before us was occasioned by an attempt on the part of the government to meet his representations. I do not know whether or not they have, but at least I am quite sure he was making very vigorous representations. It may well be that the consideration of this subject had been before the government for some time, in view of the interest which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has in it. I know that there are other members in this house extremely interested in this subject. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has already discussed the matter on different occasions. These members have expressed their opinions, but what I am pointing out is that reference has already been made this afternoon to representations made by the Saskatchewan legislature. I believe that the committee should not be tied on this matter but that

Redistribution Committee they should be free to consider the representations of the government of Saskatchewan. If they are to consider those representations the figure should be 10 per cent and not 15 per cent, because that was the figure stated in the resolution adopted by the Saskatchewan legislature.
Most certainly if I were supporting this resolution in its general form, I would wish the figure of 10 per cent to be substituted for the figure of 15 per cent. But there are other considerations. The very fact that the Saskatchewan legislature has passed a resolution, and that the effect of that resolution has been presented to this government, the fact that the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) has this afternoon raised' a question about Nova Scotia and that questions have already been raised about Manitoba, suggests that this is not a matter which affects any one province. It is a subject that affects every province and the people in those provinces.
The Prime Minister says the people of those provinces are represented by members in this house. He went further and said that this had always been the position of his party. I must take issue with that, Mr. Speaker, because 1 am under the impression that until 1946 the position of his party was the very opposite. I think we are confronted here with a question as to whether there is or is not a provincial interest affected. If there is a provincial interest affected, should the provinces be consulted? I should like to quote the words of an earlier leader of the Liberal party in Canada, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. In 1907, as reported at page 2198 of volume II of Hansard for that year, he had this to say:
The question we have to deal with at the present moment is this. In parliament here we can do as we please; we are in the majority; but are the members of this house prepared to say that if any province finds itself aggrieved by the terms of confederation, which have been accepted by all the provinces, they will ask the British parliament to alter the constitution in the way desired by that particular province? Such a course might be followed by very serious consequences. Confederation is a compact, made originally by four provinces, but adhered to by all the nine provinces who have entered it, and I submit to the judgment of this house and to the best consideration of its members, that this compact should not be lightly altered. It should be altered only for adequate cause, and after the provinces themselves have had an opportunity to pass judgment on the same.
In those words, Mr. Speaker, Sir Wilfrid Laurier was reiterating what he had said on many earlier occasions, namely that the British North America Act is a compact, originally agreed to by the four provinces which started Canada on its course but subsequently adhered to by all the nine provinces which joined to make one great nation. Now

that there are ten provinces and that the whole of the area which might be incorporated within Canadian boundaries under the original concept of the fathers of confederation has in fact adhered to that compact, I submit that our obligation to respect its provisions and to respect the spirit of that compact is greater today than ever before.
Nor was that view expressed on behalf of the Liberal party alone. In 1914 Sir Robert Borden was speaking on a motion for leave to introduce the Representation Act of 1914. A subject similar to that which we have before us today was under consideration on February 10, 1914, when he had this to say, as reported at page 612 of Hansard for that date:
The terms which were then fixed between the four original provinces undoubtedly constituted a compact between those provinces, and up to the present time they have, of course, been carried out according to the true intent and meaning of the statute.
Sir Robert Borden then dealt with further developments by way of adding new provinces. He had this to say, as reported on page 614 of the same volume of Hansard:
Speaking for myself, I do not see how it would be possible for this parliament to attempt any alteration in the representation of the provinces without the consent of the provinces themselves. It was in that connection that the question was taken up before the interprovincial conference held last autumn in the city of Ottawa, and the result of the proceedings of that conference amounted to this, that the conference declined to take any action on the subject, saying that the matter was one for the consideration of parliament. It is absolutely, in one sense, for the consideration of this parliament, although this parliament has no power to amend the British North America Act. On the other hand, if I apprehend the situation correctly, so far as the four original provinces are concerned, it was also a question for these four original provinces to say whether or not any change could or should be made in the compact under which the first provinces entered into the confederation. The province of Quebec having been fixed as the pivotal province for representation retains the exact number of sixty-five members in this house under all conditions.
Then at a later date in 1924, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen had this to say as reported at page 520 of Hansard for that year:
The British North America Act and the limitations which are imposed upon our powers, if there are such limitations, are made of our own free will. There is no inferiority in that. It is the result of a treaty as my hon. friend from Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) said. It is a treaty between various colonies which entered into an agreement. They fixed what the powers of the central parliament should be, and they also fixed what the powers of the various provinces which succeeded the colonies of that time would be, and this was ratified and accepted by the Imperial parliament of the time. Everything we have or have not is because we wanted it so. Now this treaty cannot be changed, it has been the contention of many constitutional authorities, and I think it is only fair that no change should be

accepted, without the consent of all those who were parties to it. It is a sacred treaty just as is any ether treaty; it is no "scrap of paper."
Then in 1925 the house was dealing with an address asking for power for the Canadian parliament to amend the British North America Act, with the limitation that it could not make amendments affecting rights guaranteed to minorities. At page 300 of Hansard of February 18, 1925, Mr. Ladner interrupted Mr. Lapointe with a question:

speechtext:
If the minister will permit me, will
that not apply in the case of each proposed amendment? Does the minister consider it advisable to lay down general clauses which will enable the provinces and the dominion to amend the constitution, or would it not always be a question of amending the act only after consultation with the provinces?
That question was answered by Mr. Lapointe as follows:

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I submit that this should be a
matter for understanding between the dominion and the provinces, and it is a matter upon which, I am sure, agreement might and should be reached. I heard an hon. member say the other day, speaking, I believe, of the suggested law concerning the eight-hour day, and evidently being impatient of the obstacle put in the way of that enactment in the difficulty of knowing the respective fields of jurisdiction on the part of the dominion and the provinces-I heard him say, "Well, where there is a will there is a way." I was surprised at that statement. That was the spirit which inspired the invaders of Belgium in 1914, and the world was precipitated in a sea of blood. Surely the British North America Act cannot be made a scrap of paper, as that treaty was made at that time. There is a way, perhaps, yes; but the only way is the friendly way, is the legal way, is the constitutional way. It is to approach the various parties to the agreement with a view to arriving at an understanding as to the changes which may be necessary and which may be agreed upon by all the parties to the pact. As I have said, I do not think there could be any other way; I believe that any arbitrary action in the matter would simply defeat its own purpose and would strike at the root of our national unity. I think I cite history correctly when I say that every time there has been a dispute in Canada as regards provincial rights, those who were on the side of provincial rights were victorious in the end. I do not think there can be any attempt to change the mutual charter of both the dominion and the provinces by the arbitrary action of this parliament. I do not think it is possible to do it. To those who want changes, and I am willing to admit that there might be the necessity for changes, I would say that the only way to get them is the constitutional way, to ask the consent of the various parties to confederation. Mr. Speaker, after sixty years of confederation I think we may safely say that notwithstanding the great obstacles which were in their way the Fathers of Confederation who gathered in 1865 did a great work; I think we may boldly say after sixty years that their work has been a very satisfactory one. It was not perfect; there is no perfection in human devices, but certainly they did the best they could.
As I have said, I would not like to leave the impression that my own view is that no changes should be made at any time, or that no changes are possible. I agree that we are living in 1925, and not in 1865. The problems of Canada must be settled in the light of the present situation.
Redistribution Committee
Mr. Speaker, may I say that we are living in 1952, not in 1865. But again I suggest that every argument put forward by a great member of the Liberal party in this house at that time bears consideration by the members of this house today.
On the very next day following the one to which I have already referred, on February 19, 1925, Mr. T. A. Crerar, who was then the leader of the Progressive party, spoke on this subject. I wish to quote from what he said on that day as reported at page 317 of Hansard for that year:
I quite agree with the argument advanced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) yesterday that the confederation pact was in the nature of a treaty. It was the result of different provinces getting together and agreeing upon a solution that would lead them out of their difficulties. But while that was one of the reasons behind the confederation understanding or agreement in 1867, there was also another aspiration behind it, and it was voiced, perhaps most strongly, by the great architect of confederation, Sir John A. Macdonald, for in large measure he was the architect of confederation, even if he could not claim credit for originating the idea.
Then again on the same day, Right Hon. Afthur Meighen spoke as follows, as reported at page 335 of Hansard of 1925:
The resolution itself calls upon this house to petition the British parliament to give us power to amend the British North America Act by a majority vote. I have not heard any hon. member, save the mover, support the resolution in those naked terms. The speech of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is decisive in the negative. He raised only one objection-no other is needed. He laboured it, perhaps, too long, but he presented it most forcibly and well. No one in this parliament of Canada could dream, for a moment, of asking the British House of Commons and House of Lords to tear up the securities to which we and others are parties on the mere demand of this house itself. Undoubtedly, the pact of confederation is a contract and there are rights involved therein not represented by the parliament of Canada. We could not put ourselves in the position of asking that rights so secured should be disturbed on our motion alone. The speech of the Minister of Justice determines, I think, without power of dispute, that there should never be suggestion of amendment affecting other parties to the contract save after conference and consent of those other parties.
I have read those quotations at this length for two reasons, Mr. Speaker. The first was to answer the suggestion that it has always 'been the policy of the Liberal party that the provinces are represented effectively through the members here in relation to matters of this nature, and the second was to lay the foundation for an amendment I shall introduce, and which has as its purpose the redeclaration of what I believe to be the proper principle in dealing with a question of this kind.
To my quotations from Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. Lapointe and Mr. Crerar, I know that the answer may be given that in 1946 the then minister of justice, who is now the Prime

Redistribution Committee Minister, (Mr. St. Laurent) introduced another method; and that following his assertion that the provinces are all represented in this parliament, he then went on to make an argument in support of a resolution which had as its ultimate result a change in the basis upon which the provinces of Canada would be represented, without consulting the provinces themselves. I do not accept that resolution as binding or as final. I think this house followed a wrong course in 1946. I think that the house would have been well advised to adopt the amendment introduced at that time by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he sought to have the provinces consulted before the final decision was made. I believe that at that time the amendment which he introduced to the motion presented to the house by the present Prime Minister, who was then minister of justice, was not only consistent with the traditional position of the Conservative party but was also consistent with the traditional position of the Liberal party from confederation up till that time.
Either there are questions affecting the interests of the provinces or there are ftot. Certainly, the legislature of Saskatchewan think that there are questions affecting their interests. It is certain from what we have already heard in this house that there are those in Manitoba who think their interests are affected. It is certain from what we have heard in this house that there are those who think that the interests of Nova Scotia are affected. It is certain from what we have heard from other hon. members in this house that the interests of all provinces are affected. And there is another reason why I think that consideration should be given to the position of the provinces in this matter.
The representation of the four original provinces was based upon the Quebec resolutions. The province of Quebec was used as the arithmetic basis upon which computations would be made, and, for the purpose of determining the representation of all provinces, the province of Quebec was to have 65 members. In 1946 that number was increased. I am not questioning at this time the desirability of the increase of the number of seats in Quebec or in any other province; but I do challenge the wisdom of making a change at this time without consulting the provinces, and I challenge still more strongly the wisdom today of making any other changes at this time without consulting the provinces, because it is apparent that further changes in the number of seats affecting the larger provinces are going to have serious consequences for the provinces with smaller populations because of the immense growth of

population in the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia and Alberta.
Nothing would be unnecessarily delayed by calling the provinces into consultation at this time and having their representations right here in Ottawa. It is possible that the provincial governments would be quite satisfied to place their views before a select committee set up by this house. Nevertheless, whatever system is adopted should be a system which would be satisfactory to them.
We will support a separate resolution setting up a select committee, and would hope that that would be introduced without any unnecessary conditions attached to it. Then it would be possible for a committee to proceed with the basic work and have representations made to it, either directly from the provinces or from a conference jointly representative of the dominion government and the provincial governments. One of the reasons why it would seem wise to follow such a course at this time is that the Minister of Agriculture, who has already indicated his interest in this proposal, thought that finality had been reached in 1946 at the time when the hon. member for Lake Centre was pointing out the desirability of consulting the provinces. The Minister of Agriculture was quite satisfied not to follow that course, and he felt that finality had been reached. I quote from what he said on this subject at page 2475 of Hansard of June 13, 1946:
This resolution provides for an amendment to the constitution which retains the membership of the House of Commons at exactly the same figure when we have forty million people as it provides for at the present time when we have less than twelve million people. In other words, the membership of the house would not under this resolution ever increase beyond 255. It would remain at that throughout all time until someone undertook to amend the constitution further in order to provide for something else. But we in this parliament cannot take into consideration all the things which people may do fifty years hence, or all things they may do even twenty years hence. We can only act in the light of the information and the knowledge we have and do the thing which we think advisable. Under this resolution what we are proposing as advisable is to have the House of Commons composed of 255 members, and we are providing the means under which it will not increase beyond that figure but will remain at it.
I should point out that the increase to 262 resulted from the addition of Newfoundland as the tenth province of Canada; but that in no way changes the effect of the words of the Minister of Agriculture in this house on June 13, 1946. May I remind hon. members that no matter what the Prime Minister thought then, no matter what the Prime Minister thinks today, the Minister of Agriculture had this to say:
It would remain at that throughout all time until someone undertook to amend the constitution further in order to provide for something else.

Unless the Minister of Agriculture has some new opinion in regard to this matter, it is clear that he would support the position we take, that this is a subject upon which the provinces should be consulted, and most certainly that there must be an amendment to the British North America Act. If there is to be an amendment to the British North America Act to change the number of seats in this house, then I do submit that, no matter what was done in 1946, we should go back to the principles accepted by the Liberal party for many long years, as stated by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and later by Mr. Lapointe and by other Liberals as well, and recognize that the agreement between the provinces-call it a compact, call it a treaty, call it a covenant, call it an agreement, call it what you will- did represent the basis upon which the provinces of that day agreed to form one nation, and the basis upon which all the other provinces which have joined this nation since that time have entered confederation.
I can only repeat what I said before. If we were to deal with a resolution which introduced the figure of 15 per cent as the limit of reduction of the number of seats of any province, we would be partially recognizing the request that has been made: whether it came first from members from Saskatchewan, or not, or whether it came first formally from the government of Saskatchewan, wherever it came from, it goes partly along the road toward recognition of their recommendation but does not go the whole way. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if the committee is to give consideration to matters of this kind, this house should not tie the hands of the committee by dealing with the figure of 15 per cent. It should be quite ready to consider the resolution presented by the legislature of Saskatchewan, and have before it that resolution in its original form, asking that 10 per cent be the figure which would be the maximum reduction in the number of seats in that province.
What the committee will do will then be obviously for it to decide, as it will be for this house ultimately to decide what it shall do, following the report of the committee itself. I do urge that in a matter of this kind it be recognized that while today Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick may be concerned about the effect of the law as it now stands, it might be any other province at some other time-yes, it might be Quebec or Ontario or British Columbia at some time in the future. I do not think we should deal with this on the basis of casual expediency, seeking partly to meet requests for justice which have been made by one province or another, and then
Redistribution Committee limiting the measures to which concession is made to the request put forward by any provincial government.
I think this is the time to bring all the provincial governments together, recognizing that those provincial governments-or certainly some of them-were not satisfied with the course followed in 1946, and with that knowledge seek a basis for redistribution which would be satisfactory not only to members of the House of Commons but to the people of Canada generally, as well as to the provincial legislatures representing the people in the provinces within the provincial sphere, as do members of the House of Commons representing the people of the whole of Canada within dominion jurisdiction.
Before I move the amendment I am about to propose, may I anticipate any suggestion that this will delay matters. If the amendment I offer is adopted by the house, then a motion to set up a select committee can be put forward, the committee can be set up and can be dealing with the routine procedure and the basic material connected with this subject, while independently a conference can be held which would seek the opinions of the ten provinces and some basis which would accept the sanctity of the British North America Act .as the great agreement which laid the foundation for Canadian unity.
Therefore I move in amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"whereas there is presently before parliament a bill to provide for representation of the House of Commons which inter alia allots to the several provinces of tile dominion the number of members they may elect to the said house;
And whereas it has been represented to the government and parliament of Canada that provision should be made for minimum representation of individual provinces:
And whereas provision for such minimum representation cannot be made without first amending the British North America Act;
And whereas the British North America Act interpreted in statutory form the agreement made by the four original provinces and subscribed to by all the other provinces on entering confederation,
Therefore be it resolved that in the opinion of this house appropriate steps should be taken for dominion-provincial consultation so that the views of the several provinces may be made known to this house before consideration is given to changing their electoral representation as presently provided by the British North America Act."

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, now that the amendment has been disposed of, I rise to speak to the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). As I see it that motion and the debate which has developed thus far raise three main questions. First is the question as to what is the best and most desirable way to tackle the problem of redistribution. In the second place we have before us the precise terms of the Prime Minister's motion, which we must consider and on which we must express our views. In the third place we have the constitutional question which I submit is in fact raised by the motion and has also been raised in the course of the debate by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). My remarks may involve some crossing of the lines between those three questions, but at any rate they are the three points to which I wish to address myself at this time.
In the first place I want to express once again as strongly as I can the view of this group that redistribution should not be the business of parliament nor of a parliamentary committee. We share to the full the views which have been expressed on a number of occasions by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) to the effect that redistribution should be handled by an independent commission.
The last time redistribution came before this house was in 1947. Parenthetically, I might point out that it was in 1946 that a resolution seeking an amendment to the British North America Act was passed so as to change the basis of redistribution, but it was in 1947 that the redistribution bill itself came before us. On the second reading of that bill in 1947 I moved an amendment to the effect that the bill be not then read a second time but that the house express as its opinion the view that the whole question of redistribution should be dealt with by an independent commission. One of the first members to speak after I moved that amendment was the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). He pointed out that this idea of an independent commission was an old one so far as he was concerned, and that he had in fact prepared a bill in that direction some years before when he had been a member of the government. He referred to that bill again in a speech he made in the house during the course of this session.
In other words, in 1947 the member for Quebec South indicated his support of the principle of the proposal contained in my amendment to the second reading of the redistribution bill, but he pointed out that it was too late then, when redistribution was on our doorstep, to consider any other method
Redistribution Committee o.f dealing with it. I was therefore disappointed that the member for Quebec South, having said that when redistribution is on our doorstep is no time to deal with the problem but that it should be dealt with in between, waited from 1947 until redistribution was on our doorstep again before he raised the matter in this house, either by a speech or by the bill he has placed on the order paper. I agree with him that this problem should be dealt with by an independent commission, but I feel that this business of forever saying there is some other time to deal with it is irresponsible. There is no time like the present for parliament to take a stand on this important question. Thus it is that with respect to that part of the Prime Minister's motion, Mr. Speaker, which takes it for granted that it is proper to refer this matter to a committee of this house, I am in disagreement.
The other day when the member for Quebec South was speaking, he had occasion to quote from Professor Norman Ward of the university of Saskatchewan, who has written quite a number of articles and works on parliamentary democracy and in particular has recently written a number of articles on the redistribution question. One of those articles appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of February 9, 1952 and was entitled "Too big for parliament." I should like to quote a few sentences from that article.
The problem of redistribution has become too vast and complicated to be handled satisfactorily by a committee of the House of Commons, which, like all house committees, has no staff trained in research techniques or anything else. With the best will in the world, a group of M.P.'s drawn from many occupations, provinces and political parties would find it extremely difficult to face objectively the problems connected with sharing seats fairly among the provinces and sharing seats fairly among the people within each province. Population density, homogeneity and topographical features and area, are all factors which ought to be considered seriously. But under the normal circumstances in which redistribution takes place in the House of Commons, with all parties jockeying for position, all factors become entangled in what Hon. C. G. (Chubby) Power, M.P, who ought to know, has called an "unseemly, undignified, and utterly confusing scramble for personal and political advantage."
I agree with what the member for Quebec South has said, and I agree with the views expressed by Professor Norman Ward in his advice to us that this problem should be dealt with not by a committee of those who are interested in the boundaries of seats for which they are potential members in future parliaments but rather by an independent commission.
I would point out that most democratic countries have moved on to the idea of an independent commission, and in particular I

Redistribution Committee draw attention to the practice that has been in vogue at Westminster since about 1916 or 1917. It was at that time that a conference of members of all parties in the British House of Commons was convened to go into this whole matter. They recommended the appointment of an independent commission to deal with the problem. This conference recognized that there should be an element of parliamentary representation, but the recommendation confined that element to the Speaker of the British House of Commons. Although the reports of the boundary commission of the United Kingdom are subject to perfunctory approval of the British house, nevertheless any changes that have been made in the boundaries in the United Kingdom since that time have been made by that independent commission. I feel that we, as members of this House of Commons, owe it to this country to take steps as speedily as we can in the direction of setting up an independent commission to deal with this matter.
I should like to point out that in the quotation I read from Professor Norman Ward, he referred not only to the impossibility of members of parliament dealing objectively with the problem of sharing seats within a province, but he said it was equally difficult for members of parliament to be objective in sharing seats fairly among the provinces. Both of these problems, Mr. Speaker, are before us at this time. The Prime Minister's motion pinpoints the problem of sharing seats in this parliament among the provinces. If the motion passes and the committee is set up, in addition to dealing with the problem of sharing seats fairly amongst the provinces, that committee will have to deal with the problem of sharing seats fairly within each province. The latter problem is one that every redistribution committee has had to deal with, and the results are too well known to all members.
However, the main issue before us in the Prime Minister's motion is the question of whether or not members of parliament are competent to make a decision as to what is a fair way of apportioning seats amongst the different provinces of this country. I feel that we should have an independent commission, not only for the problem we have had every ten years of drawing the boundaries properly within the provinces, but we should also have an independent commission to grapple with the fundamentals of the question that has arisen because of the serious loss of seats in certain parts of this country. The question of the sanctity of the "Rep by Pop" formula is raised. Adherents of the democratic process across the years have believed in this formula. In the main there is no question but that it is a principle
tMr. Knowles.]
from which we should depart with the greatest of caution. Yet there are times when, by oversimplifying a principle, a wrong can be done. That seems to have been recognized by the Canadian parliament because we have departed from the "Rep by Pop" principle in a number of ways. We have departed from it in apportioning the seats amongst the provinces. From 1867 down until 1946 there was in the British North America Act what was known as the one-twentieth rule which very definitely varied the "Rep by Pop" principle. Since 1915 there has been in the constitution of this country the rule that no province can have fewer seats than the number of senators assigned to that province. That rule definitely upsets the "Rep by Pop" idea. On several occasions when new provinces were admitted into confederation, they were allotted members in excess of the number to which their actual population would have entitled them. That is the basis upon which Yukon-Mackenzie River was given a seat; while in terms of area all of us feel that there should be more than one member up there, nevertheless in terms of population we have upset the "Rep by Pop" rule for that large area.
Those who have advocated these various deviations from the "Rep by Pop" rule have had good arguments for them, and have always said that we should use plain, ordinary, common sense. I quite agree that there has been some common sense in some of these departures from the "Rep by Pop" rule. But, Mr. Speaker, let us honestly face up to what has been done. Let us face the fact that we have found fault with that rule from time to time and that we have found it necessary to develop certain overtones or deviations in order to deal with actual problems. That is what is happening now. In 1943 and in 1946 the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who was minister of justice on both occasions, spoke 'favourably of the "Rep by Pop" rule. I have the quotations here on the desk in front of me. Particularly in 1946, when it was decided to do away with the one-twentieth rule, the Prime Minister, speaking for the government, said it was felt at that time that we should get our representation more nearly on the basis of the population of the country.
We lay down these rules but we change them every ten or twenty years. Now, within less than a decade since the last change was made, presumably for all time, the Prime Minister is confronted with this problem created by the loss of five seats in Saskatchewan, two in Manitoba and one in Nova Scotia. He realizes that the strict application of that rule produces an unfairness or a

wrong, and so he feels-as does the government with him-that perchance consideration should be given to some variation in the rule of "Rep by Pop" in order to avoid creating an anomaly or perpetuating a wrong. If we have reached the point where we recognize, through the experience of this country from 1867 on, that "Rep by Pop" oversimplified and applied strictly does not meet the bill, is it not time that we referred this whole matter to an independent commission for a study of the basic factors involved in the representation in the House of Commons?
At this point I want to say that it is my intention to support the Prime Minister's motion. There is a change which I think should be made and which I believe would make it better, but either in its present form or with the change which I shall suggest, it is still an expedient to deal with the problem rather than the setting up of a commission to deal with the problem in terms of fundamentals.
The Prime Minister today referred to the loss of population in Saskatchewan, and yet said that that was not any indication that there was a decline in the contribution of the people of Saskatchewan to the life and the economy of this country. I agree with him. But does that not suggest that maybe we have got to take into consideration other factors besides that of population? Is that not so, particularly in a far-flung country like this, in a country like Canada where we have some areas that are thickly populated and others that are sparsely populated but are still making a great contribution to the life of this country? The situation in our land is unique and, as I say, it seems to me there are other factors than that of population that should be taken into consideration. But I think that consideration should be given not by way of a snap judgment on a resolution which is at best an expedient but rather that that consideration should be given by a really independent body studying the whole problem.
Anyone who has read works such as those of Professor Ward will realize that there is room for real study of -this problem. That study might produce a set of rules which would be satisfactory and which would make us all feel happier in that they would be fundamental and basic rather than just expedients. I want to say again, Mr. Speaker, -that I feel strongly that we should have an independent commission not only for the job that is proposed in the bill that is on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), namely the drawing of the boundaries of the constituencies within our provinces, but we
Redistribution Committee should also have it to deal with this basic and fundamental question of what should be the factors taken into consideration in deciding the representation from the various areas in this country.
A few minutes ago I was giving examples of the way in which we violate the principle of "Rep by Pop". In particular, I was doing it with respect to the division of the seats among the provinces. I might also add that within the provinces we do not worry a great deal about the principle of "Rep by Pop". There is one member in this House of Commons who represents a constituency which, according to the last census, had a population of 9,999 persons, less than 10,000, There is another member who sits two or three seats away from me who represents a constituency in which there are nearly
160.000	persons. That is a proportion of 16 to one. That is the variation in the size of constituencies in terms of population represented by members in this house. I should point out that those two constituencies are in different provinces but even in one province like Ontario, the population goes all the way from less than 20,000 to nearly 160,000.

The hon. member for Souris represents only about one-third of the number represented by those of us from the constituencies in the city of Winnipeg. In view of all that, and particularly in view of the situation to which I have referred in Ontario, where members represent constituencies with populations which run from less than
20.000	to nearly 160,000, this is no place for anyone to stand up and prate about "Rep by Pop". That situation is defended here-
20.000	in one constituency and 160,000 in another; really no one defends that extreme case, but there are members in the house who will defend variations from 40,000 to 60,000, we will say, on the ground that it is easier for a member to give service to a compact constituency like mine, for example, than it is for a member who represents a far-flung constituency that may cover half of a province. There is one constituency in my province of Manitoba that covers, in terms of area, nearly two-thirds of the province, I believe. I would be the first to admit that the member for that constituency has a much more difficult time in serving it than I have in serving a constituency that is only

Redistribution Committee a mile wide and two or three miles long. There is room for some variation in cases such as I have just mentioned, but not for the extremes I referred to earlier.
However, if we accept that principle within a province I suggest that the day has come when we are going to have to accept that principle as among the various areas in this country. Here in central Canada-shall I say from Three Rivers down to Windsor-you have an area where the population is heavily concentrated. If you look at the map of those constituencies you will find that they are all fairly small. I do not think there is a doubt in the world that members in that whole area could give service as members of parliament to a larger number of people per member than is possible, shall we say, in the whole area from the great lakes to the Rocky mountains.
I do not think it is our right as members, affected as we are, to make decisions of that kind. I think, however, that there are basic principles that have got to be gone into, and that the type of body to go into them is an independent commission with some good judges on it or some good students of this matter, such as a man like Professor Norman Ward whom we have been quoting, and others, including geographers and statisticians-people who could really look at this problem objectively. I hope that it will not be long before that approach will be made.
If the hope of getting such an independent commission to deal with this problem at this time is dim, in view of the fact that the Prime Minister has put this motion on the order paper, that means that we have to express our views on this particular way of dealing with the problem. I think I made it clear that I regard it as an expedient; certainly, a poor second to the type of proposal that I have been making. But if the independent commission is not forthcoming, what about this expedient? Well, at least it does attempt to face up to the fact that "Rep by Pop" as among the provinces, while it sounds good, does create anomalies and cases of unfairness. That is particularly true, and very obvious, when the result of the strict application of section 51 of the British North America Act results in a province like Saskatchewan losing 25 per cent of its membership at one fell blow, five seats, and the province of Manitoba losing two seats at the same time, even though we in the province of Manitoba have had an actual increase in our population in the last ten years of over 5 per cent. Well, if that is the basis-
