subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I am very happy to be interrupted by that applause for you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, and to have the honour at this time of extending publicly to you my congratulations on your recent election to the high office which you now hold.
I was about to say that the proposal that is now before us is worth consideration as a second best, in that it faces up to the problem and tries to solve it, if you accept the basis that this is parliament's job. But if we are going to deal with the problem in this way, I feel very strongly that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) should have given more consideration to the 10 per cent floor which was suggested by the resolution that was passed unanimously by the legislature of Saskatchewan.	.
I do not take the view of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) that because the legislature of Saskatchewan passed the resolution that means that it has to be presented as it is to the committee, for this is clearly a federal matter; but I still think the government should have given more favourable consideration to the terms of that resolution. I listened carefully, both on Wednesday, April 9, and again this afternoon, to the two arguments which the Prime Minister advanced against the 10 per cent floor rather than the floor of 15 per cent, and in my view both of his arguments can be answered quite easily.
First, his argument was that the 10 per cent floor would result in Saskatchewan having 18 members, and Alberta 17, despite the fact that Alberta's population is a little larger than that of Saskatchewan. Well, Mr. Speaker, that argument would have been valid on the basis of the Prime Minister's resolution in the form in which he first placed it on the order paper. But he withdrew the motion in the form in which he first placed it on the order paper, and submitted a substitute motion, which has this extra proviso to the effect that the operation of this floor must never result in a province with a smaller population having more members than some other province with a larger population. But that proviso is there now, and if he changed the figure of 15 per cent to 10 per cent in the new form of his motion-and that is what we have now, and not the original form-if he changed it in the new form the result would be that Saskatchewan would have 18 members instead of 17 or 15, and the application of the proviso would give to Alberta the same number of 18 members as would be given to Saskatchewan.

The same 10 per cent floor which I am now advocating would of course result in Manitoba losing only one member instead of two. I realize I am from Manitoba and it may be said I am speaking on behalf of my own province, but I think hon. members will have to admit the justice of this argument. I submit that for a province to gain population to the extent of 5-8 per cent and then be asked ito take a loss of two members is not fair, and that a proposal such as the one I am making that we have a 10 per cent floor so that we would lose only one seat with our 5 * 8 per cent increase in population is one to which further consideration should be given. I have been tempted to move an amendment to that effect, but you know we have the experience now and then in this house of having amendments or motions which are made from the opposition side defeated. Even when they are passed unanimously sometimes the government rejects them, but we will get to that in another debate. Therefore rather than move it in the form of an amendment, at this time at any rate, I put this 10 per cent proposal forward as a suggestion and I ask the Prime Minister to consider it seriously.
I say to him again that his first argument against the 10 per cent floor was an argument that he thought up and was valid in relation to the original form of the motion, but it is not valid in relation to the present form, because the result would be as I have indicated, of Saskatchewan retaining its 18 seats. It would result as well in Alberta having 18, and Manitoba would end up with 15 which, as I say, is a loss of one seat. Surely, that is loss enough for us to take when we have had an actual increase in population to the extent of 5 [DOT] 8 per cent in the last ten years.
The other argument that the Prime Minister used against the 10 per cent floor was that it would provide in effect a floor for Newfoundland of its present 7 seats. It is obvious that that is what it would do. If you had the 10 per cent floor a province with 7 seats could not lose one member, and so 7 would be the floor. The Prime Minister said that that would give it a floor higher than the other maritime provinces. I think he meant that it would be a floor higher than the floor of the other maritime provinces. But that does not apply except in the case of Prince Edward Island. New Brunswick already has a floor of 10; Nova Scotia also has a floor of 10. Prince Edward Island has a floor of 4, but that is two above the number of members it would be entitled to mathematically. I do not think it would be unfair for Newfoundland, as a result of the 10 per cent formula, to have a floor of 7. Wha* is so sacred about those senatorial floors? I would say that we
Redistribution Committee should not disturb them in the sense of reducing them, but there is no law against providing a higher floor above the present floor, which is what even the present 15 per cent clause could do with respect to some of the provinces eventually.
But let me get back to the senatorial floors and to the situation in the maritime provinces. If you were to take the present population of Prince Edward Island as a basis for its senatorial floor, or for its floor of 4 in the number of members of parliament it must have, on that basis New Brunswick's population is such that it should have a floor of 20, Nova Scotia a floor of 26, and Newfoundland a floor of 14. On the other hand, if you were to leave out Prince Edward Island because of its very small population and take New Brunswick on the basis of its present population and say that its present population entitles it to a floor of 10, on that basis Nova Scotia would be entitled to a floor of 12 and Newfoundland to a floor of 7. So, Mr. Speaker, on no count can you make it out that it is unfair for Newfoundland to have a floor of 7 rather than its present floor of 6, particularly when Nova Scotia and New Brunswick already have their floors of 10. I might also point out that a 10 per cent floor under the reduction to be effected as a result of any census would also provide a floor of 9 for the western provinces. I cannot envision a day when the mathematics of the situation would reduce us down to that figure. At the present time the senatorial floor is not much use to us out there. It gives us a floor of 6 in each western province. If we had a 10 per cent floor that at least would give us a floor of 9 rather than the present floor of 6.
And so, on all counts, I do not see any argument at all against the resolution submitted by the legislature of Saskatchewan. I strongly urge the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to reconsider that part of his motion. He might consent even to someone on his side amending his motion, not necessarily changing the 15 per cent to 10 per cent, but putting both figures in, and thus giving the committee the right to consider both propositions, as alternatives. Surely that is little enough to ask.
As I say, I am not, at this stage, moving an amendment. Rather I make this suggestion to the Prime Minister, because if we are going to follow this method, this use of an expedient, that of having a floor in terms of percentage, then I think we are fully justified in asking that it be 10 per cent rather than 15. And I plead for that, not only

Redistribution Committee for my own province, which it would certainly affect, but for the province of Saskatchewan and other areas that might be affected now or at any time in the future.
I turn now to the constitutional aspect of the question, touched upon by inference by the Prime Minister and touched upon very directly by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). I would point out first that since confederation there have been four amendments to the British North America Act which dealt directly with the problem of representation or redistribution. Those four amendments are the amendments of 1886, 1915, 1943, and 1946.
The amendment of 1886, which is dealt with at page 99 of Dr. Ollivier's book, in which he deals with the British North America Act and Selected Statutes, was an amendment giving the parliament of Canada the right to provide for representation in the House of Commons-and the Senate, too, if they wished-from territories not included within the provinces. That certainly affected representation in the House of Commons and also affected the ratio as between any one province and the rest of the country.
The amendment of 1915, which is dealt with at page 111 of this same volume, is the amendment which dealt with the senatorial floor. It now operates in the case of Prince Edward Island, and certainly did have and still has a bearing upon the representation in the House of Commons, and the ratio of seats among the various provinces.
The amendment of 1943, which is dealt with at page 118 of this same volume, was one which most of us will recall as having postponed the redistribution which was to be made following the census of 1941. The result of that amendment was that the election of 1945 was fought on a redistribution worked out on the basis of the census of 1931. In effect it was contrary to the original provision of the constitution. So there again was a constitutional change having a bearing upon representation in the House of Commons.
The last of the four to which I have referred is the amendment of 1946, to which reference is made at page 119 of this same volume. It is the amendment that provided a membership of 255-that was before Newfoundland came in-and made provision for the basis upon which we are now operating.
There are other amendments to the constitution which might be said to have a bearing on representation. I refer to the statutes which brought in the various provinces- Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and so on, and, more recently, in 1949, the amendment bringing in Newfoundland. In each case we added members to the House of Commons
IMr. Knowles.]
and upset the ratio or the relationship which previously existed between any one province and the rest of the country.
I would point out however that in all these cases the changes in the constitution were made on motions of this parliament and this parliament alone. I wish to speak particularly with respect to the four that directly affected redistribution, namely the amendments to the British North America Act made in the years 1886, 1915, 1943 and 1946.
As I said before, in not one of these cases was there any consultation with the provinces. The changes were made here, by this parliament, on the basis of section 51 of the British North America Act which says, quite clearly-and this is the wording as provided by the Statute Law Revision Act of 1893:
On the completion of each decennial census the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such manner and from such time as the parliament of Canada from time to time provides.
In other words this was not something that was to be discussed with the provinces. This was a matter to be dealt with by the parliament of Canada. I would point out that parliament has taken it to be its right, under section 51, not only to change the boundaries within the provinces by the method we have followed, but also to change the rules governing the apportionment of seats among the provinces. That has been done with respect to each of the four amendments to which I have referred, as well as with respect to amendments admitting the various new provinces.
What was the record with respect to the attitude taken by parliament and, if you will, taken by the various parties in the house, on each of those four occasions? Perhaps that would be a good question for me to answer when we resume at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had just referred to the fact that there have been four amendments to the British North America Act dealing directly with the problem of redistribution. I pointed out that those were in 1886, 1915, 1943 and 1946. I ended my remarks at six o'clock by asking the question as to what had been the attitude of the house toward those changes on each of those occasions. May I say that on not one of these occasions were the provinces consulted. The action of sending a resolution to Westminster was taken by the parliament of Canada under

the terms of section 51 of the British North America Act. On the first two occasions, 1886 and 1915, Conservative governments were in power. The first one was during the regime of Sir John A. Macdonald. The second one was during the days when Sir Robert Borden was prime minister. The third and fourth occasions were when a Liberal government was in power, Mr. Mackenzie King being the prime minister at both times.
It is true, as was pointed out this afternoon by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), that in 1946 the Progressive Conservative party in this house opposed seeking an amendment to the constitution with respect to redistribution without first consulting the provinces. Nevertheless by an overwhelming vote of the house it was decided to amend the constitution in that way in the belief in the minds of the majority that this parliament had the right to do so under the terms of section 51 of the British North America Act. That leaves one other case, namely, that of 1943, when the British North America Act was amended in order to postpone the redistribution consequent upon the census of 1941. The result of that amendment was that the election of 1945 was fought on the basis of the census of 1931, clearly contrary to the spirit and the provisions of the original constitution. When the 1943 amendment came to a vote in the house on July 5 of that year it carried by a vote of 115 to 9. The group of nine consisted of a few then independent or semi-independent members from the province of Quebec, but all the Progressive Conservatives who were then in the house voted for the resolution to amend the constitution at that time in respect of redistribution.
Let me read a few of the names that are listed amongst those voting for the motion. Since they are listed here by their names I think it is in order for me to read them that way. The following names appear: Black, Cardiff, Casselman, Diefenbaker, Graydon, Green, Ross, Tustin, and many others. In other words, I am simply pointing out that on that occasion there was no question so far as the official stand of the Progressive Conservative party was concerned. They supported this change in the constitution having to do with redistribution.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, section 51 of the British North America Act is clear. Redistribution is a matter that comes within the responsibility of the federal parliament. The precedents, all four of them, are equally clear, namely, that the changes made in the constitution dealing with redistribution have been made by the parliament of Canada without consulting the provinces. I feel that is the course that it is still the right and the duty of this parliament to pursue.
Redistribution Committee
There is one other matter I should like to deal with briefly. The question has been raised both by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and by the Leader of the Opposition as to how we would go about a move of this kind assuming that it does involve a change in the constitution. To my way of thinking there is no doubt but that a change such as is suggested in the Prime Minister's motion does involve changing the constitution, whether that change is made indirectly or directly. After all, section 51 of the British North America Act now stipulates the basis upon which the membership of the House of Commons is to be determined. If the committee set up by virtue of this motion recommends some other basis then that is either repugnant to the constitution or involves changing the constitution. We now have the right to do that in this parliament, and we have had that right since the fall of 1949. As hon. members will recall, in the first session of this parliament-which met in the fall of 1949-we passed a motion which resulted in an amendment being made at Westminster whereby sub-section 1 of section 91 of the British North America Act now gives to the parliament of Canada the right to amend our own constitution with respect to matters that are clearly federal except for a few items specifically listed as entrenched clauses. Therefore we now can do what was done in 1886, 1915, 1943 and 1946. We can amend the constitution with respect to redistribution but, unlike what had to be done in those years, we do not now have to go to Westminster. We can do it ourselves right here in the parliament of Canada.
If I may say so, I think the method to be followed has been indicated to the house in another bill on the order paper in my name having to do with the quorum of the House of Commons. A study of that bill will make it clear that we do not have the right in this parliament to amend a statute of another country, namely, the British North America Act itself, but after all the constitution of Canada does not consist only of the British North America Act. It consists of a number of statutes, some of them British, some of them Canadian, some of them pre-1867, some since 1867. After all, Magna Carta, the Bill of Rights of 1688 and many other statutes are in effect part of the constitution of Canada. Dr. Ollivier tells me what we now have the right to do by virtue of the new subsection 1 of section 91 of the British North America Act is to pass Canadian legislation which, when added to that body of statutes comprising our constitution, does in that way amend the constitution of this country.
1443	HOUSE OF
Redistribution Committee Therefore it seems to me we can deal with this matter in either one of two ways. We can do it in an indirect way which I think is second best. We can pass a bill changing the representation of the house in which we include a preamble saying that notwithstanding the provisions of section 51 of the British North America Act, and by virtue of the power contained in section 91 (1) of the British North America Act, we enact as follows. Then we can spell out the proposed redistribution as planned by the committee. However, I feel that the better way to deal with the matter would be for us first of all to pass legislation amending section 51 of the British North America Act in the same way that my Bill No. 179 seeks to amend section 37 of the British North America Act with respect to the quorum of the House of Commons. Having amended section 51 of the British North America Act in that way to provide, as is our right, a new basis for adjusting the representation in the House of Commons, we could then bring in a redistribution bill based upon the provisions of the amendment to the constitution which we had properly enacted in the way I have suggested. If a change is to be made I hope such a course will be followed.
I thank the house, Mr. Speaker, for the attention and perhaps the extra few minutes that have been given me. I repeat that I earnestly hope consideration will be given the idea of setting up an independent commission to review the whole problem, both the question of drawing the boundaries within a province and that of apportioning the seats among provinces and areas. If that cannot be done at this time by virtue of the decision of the government, we will support the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent); but once again we would make our plea to him in the strongest possible terms to reconsider the figure set out in that motion. We feel that if a floor is going to be established it would be far more justifiable, far more in keeping with fair play to all concerned, to set the floor at 10 per cent instead of 15 per cent. The proposed floor of 15 per cent would seem to have the effect of assisting only one province. A 10 per cent floor would assist at least one other province now, if not two, and other provinces in the future, and I feel that a 10 per cent floor would appeal to all as a fairer way of dealing with this problem, pending a settlement of it on a more fundamental basis, which I hope will come soon.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I listened with great interest to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on April 9, and again to all that was said this afternoon


in connection with this question of redistribution. I was a member of the last committee to deal with this matter, and I hope we may have as easy a time in 1952 as we had then. As far as Alberta was concerned we had a very pleasant time. The hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) and I got together in his office for a very few minutes, and we were the first committee to bring in a unanimous report with respect to our province, a report which I may say was accepted by the main committee and later by the house.
We in this group will support in principle the resolution that has been brought in by the Prime Minister. I am not sure that as it stands it is in the best possible form; but because we are making the laws here I feel that we can change it if a majority of the house finds it necessary and advisable to do so. For that reason we do not intend to tie ourselves down now to the exact terms of the resolution.
Three proposals have been suggested. One is the constitutional method under which Saskatchewan stands to lose five seats, Manitoba two and Nova Scotia one. I do not feel that this is quite fair to those provinces. Saskatchewan has suffered in the past and is suffering today, not because of bad weather but from floods, foot-and-mouth disease and the agricultural policies laid down by this government. It would not be right to take five seats from them now, as would be the case under the constitutional method.
The proposal by the Prime Minister that no province should lose more than 15 per cent of its seats seems an improvement on the constitutional method. But a still better method has been suggested; that is that no province should lose more than 10 per cent of its seats. Since the province in which I live would not lose any representation under any of these methods I feel that I am perhaps freer to speak on this matter than some others may be. As things stand I believe we might very well consider the 10 per cent reduction rather than the other two methods. It may be possible that some of the other provinces, the maritimes or perhaps some provinces even closer to Ottawa, are ready to take advantage of such a provision; in fact one of the eastern provinces has already taken advantage of similar legislation passed under the British North America Act. While I have no desire whatever to take away that right, I do not believe there would be any discrimination against any other part of the dominion by having this 10 per cent floor put into effect at this time.
I believe it is fully understood and recognized by the people of Canada that the west, as a part of Canada, suffers as a result of its representation here, or rather I should say

its lack of representation. We have in the west a small population in comparison with the wealth produced, but to my knowledge that has never been taken into consideration. When you want men to go overseas you go west and get the very best men to be had. When you want the best bread in the world at the lowest price in the world you go west, and you certainly get that too. When you want to collect enormous sums in income tax, especially from the farmers, you go west and get it from them. So I think we should have some little compensation to make up for some of those things.
I feel that if this matter is sent to the committee without some of the limitations imposed at the present time; if the committee will face its work in a co-operative spirit; if it will take the advice given three or four weeks ago by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) and cut out the skulduggery, a very satisfactory job can be done. I hope to be a member of that committee. I hope to do my work in a very fair manner, and I hope to have the co-operation of all the other members in the committee.
We in this group appreciate the privilege given by the Prime Minister to his followers to vote freely on this question. That is not ordinarily the case, and I hope hon. members will take full advantage of it. Somebody suggests that it may be hard to overcome habit, but members are sent here to represent their constituents and to work for their constituencies first and their parties second. That, of course, is not the rule here with the party in power, and in that the official opposition might be included. I believe that laws are made by men and women for the benefit of the community as a whole. While we in this house are supreme, I feel that we have a responsibility to all Canadians to do a fair job in connection with the redistribution of seats in the House of Commons.

I should like to take a very few minutes in this debate following what was said by the previous speaker. I am one of those who, having read history, believe the provinces should be consulted when we make changes of this kind. There has been confusion in some minds as to whether or not the provinces should be consulted about this matter of federal representation. In his statement the other day the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) laid down the principle that the allocation of seats was by provinces according to their population. Coming from Manitoba I am naturally very interested, not only in Manitoba but in all the prairie provinces. While it has been claimed that we have representation by population, that has never been altogether true. Several amendments have been made deviating to some extent from that principle.
We go back to the census of 1911 when an amendment was passed assuring certain provinces that their representation should not fall below their senatorial representation. You have Prince Edward Island with four members representing less than 100,000 people. I am not trying to quarrel with that, but I am pointing out the disparity that will exist in the prairie provinces under this proposal. I must say that I followed the arguments of the Prime Minister very closely. I was rather impressed with his argument that no one province whose population was smaller than another province should be granted members on a basis that would give more members than the larger provinces. However, as I looked into that argument, I thought there could be a lot of flaws. Even with the proposed 15 per cent formula it would mean giving Saskatchewan 17 seats and Manitoba 14 seats. This would leave a difference of some 6,430 of population per riding in those two provinces alone. I am not objecting to saving as many seats as possible for Saskatchewan, but I am pointing out the disparity that will exist between these two adjoining provinces under this 15 per cent formula. I think that would be unfair.
As was pointed out by another member from the west, it does seem unfair that when we have a gain in population of 5-8 per cent or almost 47,000 people, we should have to lose these two seats. I would think, therefore, in view of the Prime Minister's very fair statement, he might yet reconsider and introduce an amendment to his resolution whereby the 10 per cent would be applicable rather than the 15 per cent. Certainly, this would benefit Manitoba. It might

Redistribution Committee benefit Nova Scotia, and I think it would be fairer in the future, although none of us can predict exactly what will happen in future years. It was pointed out this afternoon that when you get down to the subcommittees for the provinces you find very great disparities in the population of the various ridings. Someone said that in one riding in Quebec there were 9,999 people according to the last census.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) made reference to the very small riding I have the honour to represent. I happen to have had the privilege of being a member of the last redistribution committee, so I know some of the controversies and difficulties that are experienced. I just want to take this opportunity to make a plea, especially for the prairie provinces, for some reconsideration of this formula so that the 10 per cent formula could be made applicable rather than the 15 per cent.
As was pointed out, under this proposal no harm would come to anyone and if would assist more provinces than does the 15 per cent formula. I trust that the members of the committee will deal with their duties as fairly as possible when the committee is set up. I am making this appeal at this time because we are desirous of saving as many seats for the prairie provinces as we can. While we axe supposed to have representation by population it has been recognized, not only in this country but in many other countries, that where you have a concentration of population such as in urban centres, a representative can represent a larger number of people than he should be called upon to represent in a rural area in which there is great difficulty in travelling.
[Mr. Ross (Souris) .1

In view of the fact we are now to have two members from the Yukon and Northwest Territories, I believe we have set up a good example. I am not opposing that idea. I feel it is only right that there should be two members, despite the very small population which I think is about 25,000. I believe it is right because of the geographical conditions. The same idea should be carried out for the western provinces.
The contribution that these areas make to the welfare of the whole nation should also be taken into consideration. I was happy to hear the Prime Minister say that in Saskatchewan and the other prairie provinces fewer people are producing just as much today and making as great a contribution to the welfare of this nation as had been done in the past by a greater number of people. I think that point should be borne in mind. I wish to make a last appeal to the Prime Minister to give some direction to the committee allowing them to use the 10 per cent formula rather than the 15 per cent, because it would be more beneficial to a greater number of areas than the 15 per cent would be.

speechtext:
After the brilliant exposition by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I feel somewhat diffident in speaking about this matter, but I come from that province which will probably be affected more than any other province and I suspect my people may expect me to say a word or two. At the outset may I say that this whole idea is so tangled up that I should like to make it clear that I, too, support the 10 per cent as opposed to the 15 per cent formula. In saying that, I need not say that I am opposed to the bill which we have seen, and which I think has had first reading in this house.
Under the British North America Act, and under the strict rules of representation by population, each province would be given the number of members to which its population entitled it. This appears to be fair, and it would be fair if it were adhered to, but we know it is not adhered to. The British North America Act sets forth the basis for calculating the representations according to the population of the province, but in practice representation by population is not being carried out. I have the statistics for three or four electoral districts in Canada and the number represented by an individual member varies all the way from 10,000 to 100,000. This afternoon I looked up some of those districts, and I found this. According to the 1941 census the electoral district of Welland has 93,836 of population and Glengarry, on the other hand, has 18,732. Then

going down to Quebec, we have Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm with 63,462 of population and Iles-de-la-Madeleine with 8,940. These discrepancies surely should be ironed out.
Then there is a difference in the matter of the representation of the provinces themselves. Representation by population was abandoned when the first members of parliament were admitted to this house from certain provinces, notably British Columbia, Manitoba and Prince Edward Island. Thus, these are precedents for the abandonment of the idea of strict representation by population as such. In particular, Prince Edward Island is favourably and particularly protected by the abandonment of that principle which is and indeed should not be the sole determinant.
Then we come to the size of the territories over which a single member has care and to the interests of whose people he must attend. While I have with me no statistics in regard to this matter, I would say that in the west the large constituency is the rule and not the exception whereas in the east we have the exactly opposite position. I think someone has mentioned the comparative wealth-producing ability of those particular areas. We find this thinly populated area of the west and we know the reason for that loss in population. We know, for instance, that in Saskatchewan it is one of the greatest problems, if not the greatest. It is a problem which has been caused by the mechanization of the agricultural industry, as a result of which one man or a man and a boy can take off more wheat in these days than could a crew of 26 or 36 men some years ago. That does not mean, however, that the amount of wealth which those areas are producing is less than that which was produced by the larger number of workers.
. If one looks at the map, particularly, of, shall we say, that bend in the St. Lawrence river and including the city of Montreal, and counts the number of members in that area as compared with the number in that vast territory in the west, I think he will appreciate what I mean. If we are now to reduce the number of seats occupied by western members, we shall aggravate rather than help that condition which I have just described; for obviously such alteration would aggravate that situation in the west, and would make large areas into still larger areas to be represented by individual members. I often think that if some of the members representing city districts in Montreal, around Toronto or in some of those other thickly-populated areas, had to look after districts such as Maple Creek in Saskatchewan or Skeena in British Columbia 55704-92J
Redistribution Committee or some of these other places, they would realize what a tremendous task confronts a member of parliament for such places.
As I said, certain provinces have had their interests protected by artificial means. When I say "by artificial means", I mean by principles other than that of representation by population. Saskatchewan and Manitoba have never had that protection nor have they it at the present time. The one-twentieth clause or the 5 per cent clause-the clause which says that there should be no diminution of seats unless there was more than a 5 per cent diminution in the population-was, I think, designed, as a matter of fact, to help the maritime provinces; but the province which benefited-and I do not know to what extent the maritimes benefited-was the province of Ontario.
Adherence to the principle of representation by population would have lessened Ontario's seats by these figures: from 82 to 81 after 1921 and to 78 after 1931. Instead of that happening, that province held 82 seats from 1914 to 1947. That protection is not at: present available to Saskatchewan. Then we have New Brunswick whose representation cannot drop below 10 members of parliament and Prince Edward Island whose representation cannot drop below the number of 4. I am not saying anything against it, but of course it is over-represented at the moment in that it has four members whereas its population would justify the possession of only two. One protection is that a province cannot have a lesser number of members of parliament than of senators. But that provision certainly furnishes no immediate protection for either Saskatchewan-or Manitoba-which, on a consideration of population alone would lose -and it has been mooted; it was mooted in the bill-at one blow one-iquarter of its total representation. I do not think there is anyone in this house who thinks such a thing should happen. I am pleased to see that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) does not think it should happen either. But we are afraid that when that bill is submitted to the committee, the committee might report favourably upon it.
I agree with those who do not believe that the work of redistribution should be done piecemeal. I agree with what many of my hon. friends have said when they have indicated that it should be a matter of national consideration by those who have nothing to gain or nothing to lose by the particular transaction; in other words, that it should be a work for scientists, technicians, statisticians, geographers and perhaps particularly for men who know something about political science.

Redistribution Committee It is my opinion-and I say this without malice toward anyone-that I do not think that members of parliament are particularly qualified to do that particular job; and in saying 'that I am leaving quite out of consideration the idea of any prejudice which they might have. But since we are deprived of the benefit for the moment-because there seems to be no immediate prospect of having a committee of that kind, but I hope that it will be set up in time for the next redistribution-in the meantime we have to follow expediency and do the best we can. Coming from Saskatchewan I am naturally interested in seeing that Saskatchewan should hold, as far as possible, the representation which it now has. Saskatchewan has already suffered in the matter, as indeed has Manitoba. Owing to the timing of the election in 1921, an election was held there before redistribution could be brought about. So it was the redistribution which was based on the 1911 census that was carried on up until the election of 1925. Since the election was held before the redistribution of 1921, those two provinces of the prairie west were deprived of 7 seats for at least four years. I am not saying of course that it could be prevented. I am merely showing that we have had some hardships in the past in this regard, and perhaps should have some consideration, at the present time. The fact which I have just stated surely does away at least with the argument that we must have redistribution immediately in order to do justice to the provinces of British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec, which have found their papulations increasing. In view of all this, and in view of the fact that for the first twenty-five years of this century those prairie provinces were systematically under-represented, owing to the rate of immigration into them-I am talking now about the government of 1921 which knew that the prairie provinces were under-represented; I shall not quote the passage I have in mind, but it is clearly shown in the remarks of Mr. Meighen, the prime minister of that day, which can be found at pages 38 and 39 of Hansard of the year 1921-I, like other members who represent not only Saskatchewan but all of that prairie west, hope that at least there may be an option as between the 10 per cent and the 15 per cent which the committee can study and report on.
I like the idea too that it is not only Saskatchewan that will be favoured by any such decision. As I understand it, the province of Alberta would gain one by such a decision, and also the province of Manitoba. As I understand it, the whole prairie section would receive some benefit.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister introduced this motion he pointed out that it dealt with a matter which concerned the individual members of the house, and one which they could deal with in accordance with their own conscience. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Caldwell) to the contrary, I can assure you, sir, and through you the house, that the few words that I have to say would have been uttered in about the same language whether or not that declaration had been made. It is written: "Blessed are the meek; for they shall inherit the earth." I think that we in Manitoba have, over a period of years, taken that text a little too literally, and we are finding it out from time to time. This is another example of the truth that it is poor consolation to have title if you cannot get possession.
I am not to be trapped by my own words into opposing a compromise which will secure for western Canada two members which it would otherwise lose, and gain an additional member for the western area through the territories; but at the same time I am not to be understood to believe that the suggested recommendation to the committee goes far enough to satisfy me, or indeed, in my view, to do justice to a part of this country which has made its contribution, and which now in this compromise is left outside.
I think I have been have here long enough to suggest that so far as I am concerned the compromise suggested by this motion-acceptable as it is in part-is subject to criticism on the ground that it departs from what we had accepted as fixed procedure without general application. It is something commendable in itself, but it does not go far enough. In other words, to me it has something of the unbalance of a half measure. As a matter of fact the proposition reminds me a little bit of Jack Horner's pie. Everybody who stands to gain as a result of the present redistribution will find his plum in the pie. There is even one for the territories, and again I say that I concur in that.
British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec are being asked to make no sacrifice. Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Newfoundland are entrenched in their present position. Alberta has no interest at the moment except should it develop as a result of the committee being permitted to recommend the 10 per cent regulation rather than

the 15 per cent one. Saskatchewan will stand to gain at least something from this compromise.
If I wanted to be critical of the arguments which have been used in support of this compromise, I think I would base the criticism of the arguments on the fact that whenever this situation arises in redistribution, whether it be within a province itself or whether it be in the dominion as a whole, we are faced with the suggestion that we are bound by some shadowy thing which is called representation by population. Anyone who has been here as long as I have-not many have been here longer-and anyone who has made a study of the history of this country will realize that representation by population never was anything but a political slogan, and has no reality either at the present time or in that plan which is projected for the future.
I do not think that in any method of redistribution it is possible to be absolute in the application of principle, any more than it is possible to be absolute very often in the application of any other principle in our daily endeavours here. There are factors in this suggestion which seriously violate the principle which is basic to the concept of representation by population; factors which make it possible to have a disparity of two or three members, depending upon which of these expediencies is used, in two provinces with less than 60,000 of a difference in population.
Consequently I rose to point out that in so far as I am concerned, having decided to compromise with the present regulations with respect to redistribution, I do not think it is good enough to make a compromise which asks no sacrifice from those who benefit by the redistribution system, and which makes no concession to at least two of the provinces which are asked to make a sacrifice. Therefore I urge that in consideration of this resolution I hope it will be possible for the committee which is to be appointed when the resolution carries-as I suppose it will-to consider not merely the 15 per cent loss proposal but to take into consideration the possibility that if we abandon the present system some consideration may be given to a 10 per cent protection for a province which has made its contribution, as my own province has throughout the years. I hope that we shall not be faced again as we were in 1921, and ten years later, with the fact of under-representation. I have no solution to offer by way of an amendment to the motion; but I do urge that the committee be empowered, in wider terms than they are now given, to consider a 10 per cent loss limit, in order that this compromise, which apparently
Redistribution Committee we have decided is to be effected, shall apply to all of those who would otherwise suffer, in comparison with the other provinces.

Mr. Speaker, I had not the slightest intention of taking part in the debate. However, a remark of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) has caused me to say only a word or two.
The hon. member said that under this 10 per cent formula Alberta would gain a seat. So far as I can see, Alberta cannot gain a seat under the 10 per cent, the 15 per cent or any other percentage formula. We have 17 seats now, and on the regular basis of redistribution we shall continue to have 17 seats. So, as we were never going to lose any seats, there is no possibility of our gaining one through any percentage application that may be made.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch), who has just taken his seat, confused me somewhat by his argument. He started out by saying something to the effect that representation by population never did exist, and that therefore it was foolish to talk about it as a principle. Well, I happen to have had a couple of ancestors who suffered considerable hardship fighting for that as a principle. Therefore, for that, as well as for many other reasons, I have a considerable amount of respect for the principle of representation by population.

speechtext:
I think that principle should be maintained so far as it is reasonable and practical to maintain it. However where the hon. member for Winnipeg South confused me was when, just after making that statement, he said it should be followed in some respects-I have forgotten in just what respects.
If we are going to tinker with the constitution every time the matter of redistribution comes up-and this seems to be the modern trend, because we did it before in 1946 or 1947 and we are doing it again at this time, only a few years later-then I think our tinkering should be done with as much fairness as possible.
I do not think there is any question about it, that tinkering with this matter can only be fair if, when you desert the strict principle of representation by population, which was done in respect of Prince Edward Island in 1911, you produce a formula which will not put any province with a larger population in a position where it has fewer representatives than has a province with a smaller population. Reference was made to that situation this afternoon by the Prime Minister.

Redistribution Committee
I think that certainly should be a basic principle in any change in the constitution which is made. I have a considerable amount of sympathy with the position taken by members from Saskatchewan, that they should not lose 25 per cent of their representation at one stroke. I have considerable sympathy with their contention that they should not lose more than 10 per cent of their membership in the house at one time. But if this 10 per cent rule is put into effect, or a 15 per cent rule-and, as I say, I think Saskatchewan has some argument in favour of the 10 per cent rule-I think at the same time there should be put into effect a rule whereby this would not operate so that a province with a larger population would have smaller representation than a province with a lesser population.
Just exactly how that could be done, I am not sure. Looking at it roughly, however, I should think all that would be needed would be a provision to that effect, so that we would have a situation wherein, if a province lost 10 per cent of its population and therefore 10 per cent of its representation, and were thus reduced to 20 seats, another province with a larger population but which, under the ordinary rules, would have only 19 seats, should also have 20 seats- or 21, as the case may be.
Inevitably this would increase total representation. We must keep in mind however that the present proposal will cause a certain increase in the representation. My personal view is that it was possibly a mistake to change the base, as was done at the time of the last redistribution. We had had a base in operation since confederation in 1867. There had been some inequalities, unquestionably, chiefly through the operation of the 5 per cent or one-twentieth rule. However, by and large it had worked out reasonably well. Rather than adopt what I would describe as a slick formula in order to satisfy two provinces at the time-in 1946- I believe we would have been much better off if we had retained the old formula and, if necessary, increased the base.
If the base for the province of Quebec had been increased to 75 rather than 65 and then, apart from the maritime concession which had already been made, more or less strict representation by population had been carried out, I do not think anyone would have complained. We would have had something based upon our 'tradition, since confederation, and something which probably would still be working satisfactorily today.
The only other point I should like to make is that when the distribution of constituencies within the provinces takes place I would hope that on this occasion a more striot regard

would be had to representation by population than there was at the time of the last redistribution, so that we would not have a situation such as that described by several hon. members today wherein on the one hand there are constituencies with only eight or nine thousand people and on the other constituencies with as many as 160,000.
It seems to me that so long as we have a situation of that kind we are only giving lip service to the principle of representation by papulation. From the practical point of view, we are setting it at nought and placing some people in a situation where their votes are eight or nine or ten or fifteen times as good as the votes of people in other constituencies. That situation is not good enough. Surely the worst we should have would be a situation whereby the vote of a man in one constituency would be only half as good as that of a man in another. In other words my suggestion is that we should reach a position where discrepancies between constituencies should not in 'any case be greater than two to one.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to speak in this debate. However, since I come from a province protected by a special clause ini the British North America Act perhaps I may be forgiven if I make a few observations at this time.
It seems to me that when the question of representation is being discussed hon. members seem to feel that parliamentary representation consists only of representation by population. I am afraid I must disagree with the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) to a certain extent, because it is my view that, in addition to representation of individuals, there is the matter of representation of areas and political units. There is also the matter of representation of natural resources.
These are principles recognized in practically every parliamentary assembly in the world. Indeed, there is a certain nodding admission of this fact as it applies to representation in this House of Commons, although it would appear that in Canada we do not seem to have any regularly systematized method of dealing with the problem.
First there is the matter of representation of isolated areas. It is recognized that if an area is isolated and cut off, even though its population may be small, it would be impossible for one man to represent it properly if it is almost impossible for him to travel from one part of his constituency to another. Therefore in such cases it is thought advisable to give these isolated areas a representative of their own. In Canada the Magdalen islands are a perfect example of that very thing.

Then there is the question of the proper representation of specialized areas where there may be a minority of a particular racial extraction or even a particular religious belief, or other fairly small groups having some special interest. Their point of view can be exterminated and brought to nought by combining them with another group holding contrary opinions. Therefore in actual fact they are not represented. In many countries that condition is recognized and these minorities are given their own representation in parliament even though they are not numerous enough to make up a unit of representation.
Another most important thing to be con-, sidered is the representation of large, sparsely populated areas which, although they have small populations, are of great importance. The suggestion that the constituency of Yukon-Mackenzie River should be given two members instead of one is a practical example of the carrying out of that principle although there again there is no recognized system whereby such a principle will be followed from time to time so that on all occasions after every census the same results will be gained from a fixed formula.
There also falls in that category a principle recognized in most countries, namely, that rural areas are entitled to more representatives on a population basis than urban areas. It is interesting to realize that in this country that principle has been recognized in the past. During the redistribution of 1892, when the government of that day proposed that the representation of Montreal should be increased from three to five, Sir Wilfrid Laurier took great exception to that suggestion although even the increased representation would leave Montreal with much larger units of population per constituency than was the case in the rest of Canada. On that occasion Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
I am not prepared to admit for my part that Montreal is at all entitled to increased representation. It is admitted generally, it is admitted specifically in this bill, that there is to be a difference between the representation of urban populations... and rural populations. That object is obvious. Urban populations are represented generally to a greater degree than are rural populations, because urban populations generally furnish to rural populations many of their members . . . Montreal is represented in this house by no less than thirteen of its citizens.
That is a principle that should be recognized. New Zealand and Australia have a systematic way of recognizing it. In those countries the population of rural areas is increased by a certain percentage to arrive at the unit of representation for such areas. In New Zealand the population of a rural area is increased by 20 per cent to give a fictitious higher population than it actually has before dividing the unit of representation into the
Redistribution Committee population of the rural area to arrive at the number of its representatives. It is also generally recognized that it is much easier for a member of parliament or of any other legislative body to represent a small compact area than it is for him to represent a large sparsely populated region. Therefore in the thinly populated agricultural areas, where most people are land owners and have a real and fundamental stake in that part of the country, the unit of representation should be smaller.
Before New Zealand and Australia adopted the principle of having a smaller unit of representation for rural areas a great deal of debate was provoked in the parliaments of those countries. It was even suggested by one member of the New Zealand parliament that perhaps they should arrive at a principle of representing sheep in parliament rather than men because then they could have a fixed unit of representation which would be more suitable in its application than the representation of human beings. Someone suggested that perhaps men should represent sheep but there was no suggestion on that occasion that sheep should represent men in their parliament.
I think that the most important principle we must recognize in dealing with representation is that of the representation of political units. Almost every country in the world including Canada, although sometimes we do not want to admit it, recognizes that principle. In the British House of Commons the unit of representation for both Scotland and Wales is smaller than the unit of representation for England. They have a greater number of members than they would on a straight representation by population basis because it is felt they have certain local interests which might be discriminated against by the overwhelming weight of representation in the British House of Commons from England.
In the United States the representation of the states in congress is protected. Each state elects two senators and also sends a number of members to the house of representatives, that number depending on their population. But if the population of the state is smaller than the unit of representation it still sends at least one member. The population of New York state is many times greater than the population of Nevada. Yet they each send two elected senators to congress. As a matter of fact the population of Nevada is practically the same as that of Prince Edward Island. If the question were decided on a straight representation by population basis Nevada would be entitled to a fraction of one representative. In other words, it would be a small fraction of one constituency. In actual fact Nevada sends a member to the

Redistribution Committee house of representatives and two members to the Senate although its population is roughly the same as that of Prince Edward Island. Therefore it has a much greater relative voice in the congress of the United States than Prince Edward Island has in the parliament of Canada.
In Canada on many occasions we have recognized that principle in a sort of way, and the very system of representing provinces in parliament is proof of that point. After all, if the size of Canadian constituencies was arrived at purely on -a population basis there would be no justification for making the boundaries of constituencies coincide with provincial boundaries. If you had a fraction of a constituency left over in one province there would be no reason why you could not tack it on to a constituency in the next province, but we recognize that we should not have constituencies partly in one province and partly in another. There are provincial interests to be represented in this parliament.
Then, too, on occasion special concessions have been given to certain political areas. British Columbia and Manitoba were given representation in this parliament much greater than that to which they were entitled by reason of population when they joined confederation. As a matter of fact British Columbia was given six members in the house when on a population basis it was entitled to something less than one. Moreover there was a clause in the agreement under which they joined confederation which made it impossible for the representation of British Columbia in this house to ever fall below six.
On the other hand when Prince Edward Island joined confederation it was given only one more member than its population required. It was given six instead of five, and it was not very long before that extra member was taken away. Many of the people in the province in which I live were under the impression that on joining confederation their representation was protected, and that it would never fall below the number at which it stood when Prince Edward Island came into confederation.
The same was true of Manitoba. It was given a representation of four though on the basis of population it was entitled to only one or at the most two. It was protected in its representation for a period of time, but British Columbia's protection is permanent. Therefore I see no reason why any thought should be given, if anyone has done so, to unnecessarily cutting the representation of any province in this house. I think we are quite justified in making special exceptions in certain cases to assure that particular

political areas will be properly represented here, and that their area interests also will be protected.
That is all I have to say at this moment, Mr. Speaker, except that I would support most heartily not only the proposal to add another member for Yukon-Mackenzie, but also the suggestion that the representation from any province should never be reduced by more than 10 per cent at any one time.
Motion (Mr. St. Laurent) agreed to.

maintopic: SUGGESTED CHANGE TO KINGDOM OF CANADA
SUGGESTED CHANGE TO KINGDOM OF CANADA
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of taking the necessary steps so that this country be called the Kingdom of Canada.
He said: This resolution will not receive unanimous consent, and I was not prepared to argue it tonight because I never thought it would be reached. I shall try to convince my hon. friends on the other side of the fence that, according to tradition, they should be the first to say "Aye, aye." The introduction of this motion is a mere gesture by a minority in this country. The descendant of a great Frenchman once said that those who would be the first and last to fight to defend the British crown would be French Canadians from Quebec. Since our beloved Queen and the British government saw fit, at the time of the proclamation of Her Majesty's accession to the throne, to use the word "realm" in that proclamation, I thought this motion would be in order. Our proclamation was one day ahead of that of the British government, and obviously that is the reason our proclamation did not contain the same terms.
If one looks at a dictionary one finds that the word "realm" can be translated into French by the word "souverainete". When you translate "souverainete" into English it is "kingdom". One can see that I have, therefore, not invented anything. I do not intend to impose any invention upon my colleagues. I thought, as a member of a minority group represented in this house, that it would be a nice gesture if we in this country, having the same Queen as Great Britain but on the understanding that she is the Queen of Canada, were to step into line with the desire expressed in the proclamation. I thought also that I would please my hon. friends on the other side of the gate, because I thought they knew enough of history to realize that one of their greatest leaders, Sir John Macdonald, also desired this country be called the kingdom of Canada. One has to remember, and this is no secret, that when confederation was being discussed at Quebec and Charlottetown Sir John Macdonald thought this country should be called the kingdom of Canada. For many reasons beyond his control, it was not. I thought the Tories would grab this occasion to give to their former leader, the greatest leader they ever had not counting the one who is with us today, something that he wanted. They could line up with us and please Sir John.

maintopic: SUGGESTED CHANGE TO KINGDOM OF CANADA
speechtext: Did Sir John's ghost appear to you to instil this idea into you?

maintopic: SUGGESTED CHANGE TO KINGDOM OF CANADA
speechtext:
Did you call Sir John a ghost? We have a St. Jean, but it is St. Jean Baptiste.
Now, some members will say, "Why bring that up at this particular time when we have so many problems with which to deal which are of such great importance and magnitude? I will tell you, sir, why I brought this matter up, in addition to the reasons I have already mentioned. Looking at what is taking place in many more important assemblies, looking at all the big problems that have been dealt with with regard to conditions throughout the world, it seems to me, at least, that in many a country today if they consider trade plans, imports and exports, armaments, defence or anything which is tangible, there are some people who have thought maybe it would not be so bad a thing after all if we would pay some attention to something in some other direction; and that something in another direction is education of the masses of the people. I refer to education not only in terms of having people able to read or to write but national education or national comprehension in so>
far as national education is concerned with regard to this particular matter.
May I suggest, sir, that in the minds of the immigrants that come into this country there is a great deal of confusion, to say the least, with regard to our status. They do not know whether we are still a summer kitchen to Great Britain or to another country. Some of these people are so confused that they believe we are only a transit swing board, and therefore they wait either on the railway platform or on the pier to go to the United States. How about the next generation of these people? Even if they stay here, are they going to be in a position to teach their children that this is a country by itself; that even if we are, in the matter of trade, the third country in the world, we are adult and not merely a branch of another country, either of the United States or of Great Britain. It is no secret to anybody that since 1931, after the discussion of 1927 with regard to the Statute of Westminster, we established ourselves not only *as the third largest country in the world with regard to trade but also as a sovereign country. What is the reason, fundamentally speaking, emotionally as well as mentally, that is preventing us from establishing ourselves in the eyes of the world as being what we are? Are we ashamed of ourselves? We should do this even if only to satisfy the wish of the government of Great Britain to which we gave

Canada-Suggested Change of Name so much trouble during the last war by the confusion that was created throughout the world-with the air force, for instance, going to the four winds of the world and creating that confusion-so that people did not know that there was such a country as Canada.
I have a hunch it is a secret to our government that when the proclamation was issued it was not made by the government of Great Britain without an afterthought that would indicate to Canada that it was about time that we ourselves should do something in that direction. There may be another reason why Great Britain would like us to do that. In our international relations nowadays we have to define not only to the people within Canada- whether the old loyalists or the young loyalists-but to the outside people either in NATO or elsewhere-and I would even go a step further and say within the iron curtain-that we stand on our own feet, and everybody ought to know it.
I still remember vividly the experience of one of my friends in the press gallery who was at the time representing a London newspaper and who went to central Europe. At the meeting there he was asked what was our national anthem and what was our flag. He said that we had none. This gentleman, coming from England, was the most embarrassed man in the world. That means to say that we are creating more embarrassment to the British than maybe to ourselves. I therefore say that I would quash the idea that it is a sort of thing to satisfy our selfishness but is in keeping with the desire, as I understand1 it, of our beloved Queen and of the British government. As far as our government is concerned, I hope the membership of this house will express to our government the desire that something be done in that direction. As I said before, it is obvious that we need something of the sort in order to establish a Canadian identity, a unique front towards a unique end and also to promote Canada not only through shipments, trade and commerce, and so forth, but also to promote Canada as a nation which can be easily identified. Many people throughout the world are nowadays bewildered to see that the third nation of the world has not yet found an opportunity to establish itself without any confusion amongst the nations of the world. This occasion has been given to us by the highest authority, by our Queen and the British government, not by the member for Matapedia-Matane. I hope the house will indicate, by passing this resolution, that our government should take these steps.
Immigrants come into this country from several countries on the continent that do not know us at all. We have only to go to the


United Nations to find that out. I think the best identification we can give to the nations of the world is to establish what we are once and for all, which will eliminate a great deal of resentment even among our good friends to the south.
In my opinion there is one thing that should be borne in mind. Up to the present time we have never been able to get accepted in the Pan-American union. Why? Because the Americans think that it would mean the destruction of the Monroe doctrine. They thought that we were an annex of Great Britain. Therefore they said that Great Britain should not have a foot in that door. If that change could be brought about I believe we would be welcomed at the PanAmerican union, and that is most important.
How is it that we are accepted in NATO but we are not accepted by the nations of our own continent? Who can understand that in Europe? Who can understand it in Asia? I am sure that we shall soon be invited to form on the Pacific what we have formed on the Atlantic. If we do that these people will say:	How is it that you are welcomed
outside your own house but you cannot find a seat in the living room thereof?
There is another thing, and with this I will conclude. It is necessary for us to create a nation here as they have done in the United States. Let us call it a potpourri, a melting pot, or whatever you wish. When you meet a young boy in the United States, or an immigrant who has been there for only six months, he never says to you that he is a Czechoslovakian or a Pole; he says: I am an American. Well, let us see to it that everybody in this country calls himself a Canadian. The only way in which we can create such a spirit and a national consciousness is first of all to establish a definition of our own character, of what we are. The second thing is to try by all ways and means, as they have done in the United States and elsewhere, to create a spiritual aim for Canadians all. I remember that in 1946 I warned this parliament that if we did not have the courage to face the problem of having a Canadian flag, Quebec would soon have one. Look at what is happening in Quebec. Are we going to balkanize Canada, or are we going to unite this country and make it bigger and better, because we have more resources and more advantages than even the United States have today? Therefore I say we ought to do something toward creating that Canadian spirit. We have to take the ways and means, and this is one step in the right direction.

That, Mr. Speaker, is exactly what I am doing. I have already spoken at some length on this measure, and on various occasions. One of the ambitions which I have constantly had was to bring the matter to a vote in this house. We were fortunate in being able to do that on one occasion, and I am glad that we are fortunate again in being able to do the same thing.
I shall not take more than a minute longer, except to explain the object of this motion and to give a statement on one or two points. First, it is my idea that every child in Canada should have, in education, equality of opportunity with every other child. I am told of course that that is purely a provincial matter, and that education is purely a provincial matter. Some of my Saskatchewan friends often say to me: Why do you not get your own provincial government to give some assistance to education? Sir, I welcome assistance from our own provincial government. I have pressed the question of assistance upon them continually. I am glad that in the last day or two they have announced
Education
that they are going to give a million and a half dollars, or thereabouts, extra this year for education from some tax revenue that they have abolished for next year. In the meantime the proceeds are going to go to education. I am happy that that assistance is given to education by the province; but to me this is a national thing. This is wider in its scope than purely a provincial matter.
I am anxious that the children in every province shall have an equal opportunity of education with the children in every other province. Let me emphasize once more that we who believe in this motion have no idea whatever of imposing on any province in Canada any interference whatever with either the curriculum or the administration of education within any province. One can say that education is a provincial matter; but I should like to point out that the products of education in the various provinces are the concern of this nation. I have said before that when they go outside this country, or travel here or there within the country, they are not considered as provincial-although some speeches one hears in the house lead one to believe that that is so.
As I said before, they are considered as Canadians, whether they are bom and educated in Quebec, British Columbia, Saskatchewan or Ontario. That is all I wish to say in the matter tonight.
