speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 4, to provide for the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court of Canada in matters of divorce.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak once again in support of this bill which would give to the Exchequer Court of Canada jurisdiction in matters of divorce with respect to persons residing in provinces where there are no divorce courts. I am sure that hon. members are familiar with the terms of the bill. Nevertheless there are a few things I should like to say about it even at the risk of repeating what I have said on former occasions. In the first place, the bill does not alter any laws with respect to divorce so far as the basis for divorce in this country is concerned. In the second place, I would point out that the bill does not make available to persons in the two provinces where there are no provincial divorce courts any facility that is not now available to them.
There is at the present time available to persons residing in provinces where there are no provincial divorce courts the right to come to the city of Ottawa and obtain a divorce from the parliament of Canada. This bill, because it has in it a special clause which provides that the jurisdiction of the exchequer court in matters of divorce would have to be exercised only at the city of Ottawa, would still make it necessary for those persons to come to this same city of Ottawa. The only difference that would follow from the passing of this bill would be that those persons residing in provinces where there are no provincial

divorce courts on coming to Ottawa to seek a divorce would, instead of appearing before a divorce committee of the Senate of Canada, go to the Exchequer Court of Canada.
As hon. members are aware, my reason for introducing the bill is to provide relief for parliament from the task of processing hundreds of these divorce cases every year. There is no doubt about the attitude of members of parliament to divorce bills. We do not like dealing with them. No one feels that it is a part of the job for which he was elected. As a matter of fact, on recent occasions in this very session when votes have been called on certain divorce bills we have had the lowest attendance in the House of Commons for a vote for a good many sessions. I suggest that is indicative of the feeling on the part of a great many members that this business of divorce is not the business of members of parliament. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, all that my bill proposes is that the handling of divorces be transferred from this building and from the jurisdiction of parliament to another building in the same city of Ottawa and to the jurisdiction of a court upon which we can confer the right to deal with these divorces.
I knew before I ever came to parliament, and no one could be a member of parliament for a number of years and not recognize even more fully, how strong is the feeling in the two provinces where there are no divorce courts against the establishing of divorce courts in those provinces. I have said on two or three occasions that I think it might be argued for my bill that one of the things it would do would be to put an end to any agitation for the establishing of divorce courts in those provinces. I have read editorial comments in support of my campaign to get divorce out of parliament which have gone so far as to suggest that the matter of divorce in those two provinces should be looked after by those provinces. Well, we know that is an utterly impractical suggestion, and I should think the people in those provinces who are so overwhelmingly against such divorce courts would welcome a bill like this which would put an end to any agitation of that kind. In other words I feel that this is not only a bill to relieve parliament from the handling of divorce; it is a bill to protect the two provinces concerned from any suggestion that they should have provincial divorce courts.
I am also aware, Mr. Speaker, of the loyalty of the Quebec members in particular to the Quebec civil code, section 185 of which reads as follows:
Marriage can only be dissolved by the natural death of one of the parties; while both live, it is indissoluble.

That is part of the Quebec civil code which is part of the law of the province of Quebec, and I fully recognize it. I also recognize that the right of the province of Quebec to have maintained in force in that province the Quebec civil code is protected by section 129 of the British North America Act, and I certainly have no desire in any way to run counter to the susceptibilities or the feelings of Quebec members, or any other members, with respect to section 185 of the Quebec civil code or section 129 of the British North America Act.
I suggest that my proposal solves this problem without running counter to that section of the Quebec civil code or that section of the British North America Act. It does not set up a divorce court in the province of Quebec. If it can be said to set up a divorce court for Quebec and Newfoundland, at least it sets it up here in the city of Ottawa, where there is already a divorce court for the people of those two provinces.
I know that another argument put forward is to the effect that as matters now stand divorce has not been recognized as a right as far as the people of those two provinces are concerned. It is argued that each bill that goes through parliament is a separate law standing on its own feet; and those who oppose my bill say that in their view it is wrong in that it would establish legally in the exchequer court a right to divorce for persons in those two provinces which they do not now enjoy.
I suggest with all respect, but I suggest it for honest and serious consideration, that this is splitting hairs. There is a court now. We call it the Senate divorce committee; we call it the whole machinery of parliament, if you will, but it is there as a right of which hundreds of citizens from those two provinces are availing themselves each year. Lest anyone still try to argue that this right has not been codified and formalized I would ask hon. members to take a glance at the rules, orders and forms of proceedings of the Senate of Canada. This is a little red book corresponding to the green book we have in this house. I suppose it is red to match their carpet as green matches ours. This is not Beauchesne but it corresponds to Beauchesne, for the other place. I find that this book contains some 83 pages of their standing orders, of which 27 pages are devoted to divorce. So divorce is not just something that happens over at the other place. It is not just something that is dragged in under the provisions of standing orders relating to private bills. No; there is a separate section in the Senate manual dealing with divorce. Of 152 standing orders in the other place, 20 relate solely and exclusively
Divorce Jurisdiction
to divorce. The 27 pages devoted to divorce are made up of the 20 standing orders to which I have referred together with 11J pages of forms which are spelled out in this book I hold in my hand.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is evidence that already we have here in the city of Ottawa a recognized court for divorce for persons from the two provinces in which there are no provincial divorce courts; and I press my point that to transfer the handling of these matters from this building, this parliamentary machinery, to another building, and to the exchequer court, does not alter by one iota the present position, or introduce any facility not now available, or establish any right not already recognized, regularized, codified and spelled out in the law of this land. Since that is the situation I feel that hon. members should give pretty serious consideration to the terms of my bill.
I have said before and I repeat tonight that I am not wedded to this bill. I hope I may be pardoned for a bit of punning if I say I would even be prepared to be divorced from it if someone could show me a better way of dealing with this matter. I well recall many years ago when the present Prime Minister-at the time he was minister of justice-entered into a debate about this divorce business in which hon. members were complaining about the procedure of handling divorce bills in parliament. At that time he said to those who were complaining, "Well, if you are going to complain about the present practice, produce some other method." It was in response to that challenge that I gave some thought to the matter and came up with this suggestion for transferring the matter to the exchequer court. If anyone has a better suggestion I will welcome it most heartily. As a matter of fact if anyone has a suggestion not quite as good as mine but which would receive greater support, I would even welcome that. In other words I think my view is the view of hon. members generally, that if there is any way we can get rid of the handling of divorces as we now handle them in parliament, it would be a good move. Just as the present Prime Minister threw out a challenge when he was minister of justice to think up a better way, and as I tried to meet that challenge, now I throw out the same challenge to those opposed to this bill. I suggest that they find a better way or provide some other method, even if it is not as good, which will enable us to get rid of this business from parliament, and from this House of Commons in particular.
As I have already said, there is no doubt about the views of most hon. members on this question. Nobody really wants to keep divorce here. As for the views of the country generally, hon. members are aware of the

Divorce Jurisdiction
considerable amount of editorial comment there has been on this question, almost wholly favourable to the idea that some way other than the present method should be found. I hope we will not just continue year after year, going through the farce of passing these divorce bills in batches and droves, but that we will find a solution to the problem.
Once in a while I notice in the daily paper from my home city a little note that such and such a court granted six divorces or eight divorces. It is news that in one day a court has managed to deal with and grant five, six, eight or ten divorces. Look at what we do. We can pass fifty or a hundred. Members here have seen us pass two hundred or three hundred at one stage, and that is not even news. In this place it is only news when divorces are held up.
Again I say, Mr. Speaker, that the reluctance of members to deal with the matter, the reluctance of members even to vote on a bill when those who are opposed to divorce might actually have defeated some of the bills, makes it clear that members do not like what is going on. I suggest it is time we solved the problem by having the matter referred to some other body. Until members produce some other suggestion, therefore, I press the point that serious consideration should be given to this bill. I have already said tonight, as I have said on other occasions but perhaps as I sit down I should repeat it, that I am sure no member in this house will accuse me, in presenting this bill, of trying to ride rough-shod over the feelings or susceptibilities of persons in the provinces of Quebec or Newfoundland, or indeed over the susceptibilities of persons in any part of Canada with respect to divorce.
I have made it clear that in this bill I am not trying to change the basis for divorce. I have made it clear that I do not want to impose upon the soil of Quebec or Newfoundland any divorce court. I have made it clear that no new facility would be made available to these people. I have made it clear that we do not seek to regularize something that is not now regularized. I submit that after one has faced up to all the facts of the situation it is clear that something should be done about this matter, and until a better way is provided I suggest that serious consideration should be given to my bill. I hope that members will allow it to go to a vote and give it second reading so that it can go to a committee and be studied thoroughly.

subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Every time there is a move to grant more facilities to persons seeking divorces or a bill presented to establish another court for the provinces 
of Quebec and Newfoundland, I have been on my feet to speak against these measures. I am going to do that tonight, and I ask the house to be very patient because I must tell the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that I will do my utmost, first to stop the bill from coming to a vote tonight and, second, to try to defeat the bill. Then, I hope we shall not hear any more about this matter in the future.
The hon. member is very able, a good speaker and very persistent in his opinions. I must tell him, however, that we in Quebec, and I could include Newfoundland, might be as persistent as he is in our refusal to accept a divorce court, even it it does not sit on the soil of those two provinces. It is very easy to speak about the establishment of a court that would not be on the soil of those provinces, but the results will be the same. In granting to the people of these two provinces the right to divorce in the exchequer court, the hon. member is really establishing a new divorce court for these two provinces. Whether or not he wants it, whether or not he likes it, that is what he is doing.
In establishing a new divorce court the hon. member is granting more facilities for divorce to the people of these two provinces. To support my contention that he is granting more facilities by establishing another court, I shall quote what happened in various years in Canada when there were proposals to establish divorce courts in the various provinces. In 1875, Mr. de Cosmos, the member for Victoria riding, proposed the creation of divorce courts for the provinces. I was not in the house at that time, but some other political men were here and they opposed the establishment of those courts. When Mr. de Cosmos proposed the establishment of these courts Alexander Mackenzie said:
It is proposed to establish a court which a great number of persons are opposed to and, although I have personally no objection to the establishment of such courts, at the same time I do not desire to afford additional facilities for obtaining divorces and I hope that the resolution will be withdrawn.
Sir John Macdonald said:
I would be sorry to see any tribunal established which might be the means of inviting other dissatisfied couples to apply for divorce.
Those quotations can be found in the debates of 1875 at page 859. In 1888 Jones of Halifax put a motion asking if it would better serve the interests of the country at large if we were to establish divorce courts. At page 1414 of the debates for that year Sir John Macdonald said:
I think it would be a great misfortune for Canada to have that established.

At page 1416 Sir William Mulock said:
I think the facility with which divorces are granted in England and in other countries does go a long way to interfere with the sacredness of the marriage tie.
Mr. Northrup, in 1914 and 1916, was speaking on the jurisdiction of parliament over divorce cases when Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
For my part, I rather agree with the statement made by my hon. friend, the Minister of Justice, that up to this time, the law does not know divorce and we had better stand by that position.
I have quoted these various Canadian men to show the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that by permitting the people from these two provinces to go before the exchequer court rather than the Senate-which is an altogether different thing-he is imposing upon them a divorce court which will be called the exchequer court. These provinces have repeatedly opposed the establishment of such a court. It is quite a different thing for those in the province of Quebec or Newfoundland who want a divorce to go to the Senate. This is a special dispensation granted to the people of those two provinces who want a divorce. If you allow these people to go before the exchequer court, you have increased the facilities for granting divorces. That is what we do not want in those two provinces. I hope my hon. friend and all those who want more facilities for divorce will understand once and for all that we do not want them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Then you had better abolish the Senate.

subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
No; it is not a
question of abolishing the Senate at all. I have here figures contained in a declaration from England for the time before divorce courts were established in England. The first bill to create a court of divorce in matrimonial cases in England was passed in 1857. I am giving these statistics to prove that the establishment of divorce courts gives more facilities for obtaining divorces. During two centuries prior to 1857, only 317 divorces by act of parliament had been obtained in England. Thirty years after the' bill was passed to establish divorce courts in England -not two centuries but just thirty years- 6,381 decrees absolute for dissolutions of marriages were allowed. This is to prove that the establishment of divorce courts gives more facilities for the obtaining of divorces. In his "History of our own Times", Justin McCarthy wrote as follows:
The divorce act, judging by the public use made of it, certainly must be held to have justified itself in a merely practical sense. It seems to have been thoroughly appreciated by a grateful public. It was not easy,-
Divorce Jurisdiction
And those words are to be noted.
-after a while, to get judicial power enough to keep the supply of divorces ... up to the ever increasing demand.
That is strengthening my contention, sir, that the establishment of divorce courts gives more facility for divorces.
Gladstone said-and this can be found in Lathbury's "Letters on Church and Religion of W. E. Gladstone", volume 2, page 362-as follows:
Unquestionably, since that time (1857), the standard of conjugal morality has perceptibly declined among the highest classes of this country, and scandals in respect to it have become more frequent. The decline, as a fact, I know to be recognized by persons of social experience and insight who, in no way, share my abstract opinion on divorce.
Here is another quotation, Mr. Speaker, from a man who was in favour of the establishment of divorce courts in England. I refer to Sir Cresswell Cress well, the first judge of the new divorce court and formerly a pronounced advocate of the statute of 1857 which created it. I quote Sir Cresswell Cresswell:
I have been taught a lesson of experience. I have come to the conclusion that it is better for society to treat the marriage as indissoluble, considering it merely as a social question.
Theodore Roosevelt had this to say in the United States. Divorce courts were established in the United States and I will quote figures to prove that the more facilities there are, the more divorces there are. Theodore Roosevelt said:
Divorce is a bane for any nation, a curse on society, and a menace to home.
This is to prove from England, sir, that more courts mean more divorces, as they mean more facilities to obtain divorces. I have here the figures given to me by the bureau of statistics of the Canadian government. They are statistics for the various provinces of Canada and may be compared with the statistics for the United States. In 1941, in Prince Edward Island there was one divorce. Since the court was established in 1945 there have been 104 divorces. In 1941 the number of divorces in Nova Scotia was 68; in New Brunswick, 87; in Quebec, 48; in Ontario, 949; in Manitoba, 242; in Saskatchewan, 146; in Alberta, 311; and in British Columbia, 609. In that same year in the United States there were 293,000 divorces.
We will take the figures of 1946 in order to see the increase in the number of divorces permitted in Canada in those different provinces which I have mentioned. In 1946 the number of divorces in Prince Edward Island was 4; in Nova Scotia there were 68 in 1941 and 260 in 1946. In New Brunswick in 1941 there were 87 and in 1946 there were 382. In Quebec in 1941 there were 48 and in 1946 there were 290. We have no divorce courts

Divorce Jurisdiction
in Quebec. In Ontario in 1941, there were 949 and in 1946 there were 2,639. In Manitoba in 1941 there were 242 and in 1946 there were 636. In Saskatchewan in 1941 there were 146 and in 1946 there were 505. In Alberta there were 311 in 1941 and 962 in 1946; in British Columbia there were 609 in 1941 and 2,005 in 1946. In the whole of Canada in 1941 there were 2,461 divorces and in 1946, 7,683. More facilities and everywhere more divorces! In the United States in 1946, instead of 293,000 divorces as in 1941, there were 610,000. In 1950, in the whole of Canada there were 5,208 divorces and in the United States there were 385,000. Suppose for the moment the people of Quebec and of Newfoundland, through their members in the House of Commons, would accept the bill of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). This goes to show that unquestionably it would give more facilities for the people of those provinces to get more divorces. Unquestionably that is so. So we would have the same picture in these two provinces that they have in other countries where there are more facilities for divorce. I think, sir, that it has been shown, and repeatedly shown for a fact, for ten or twenty years, that we from Quebec do not want divorce courts. I do not see why the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre always comes back with that bill to impose on us the exchequer court as a disguised divorce court, because it would be a disguised divorce court. We do not want it, and Newfoundland does not want it either. It should be kept in mind by my hon. friend, and those who support this bill, that we do not want it.
The hon. member asked a moment ago: Well, can you give us a better way of disposing of the divorces that come before the Senate? I know that he has been building up a case for the last few weeks to show the people of Quebec, and probably the people of Newfoundland, that it would be much better to have the exchequer court deal with the divorce cases that come before the Senate. I do not say that he does it maliciously, but I understand very well. I do not believe I am mistaken when I say that he has shown much persistence in building up his case-it is very well done-to show the people in those two provinces that we should do away with the committee on divorce in the Senate, and bring the divorces to the exchequer court. I am positive that the great majority of the people in those two provinces will not fall for that. They do not like the ordinary divorce courts on the soil of their provinces, to use that term, any more than they would like a divorce court called the exchequer court
[Mr. Gauthier (Portneuf) .1
to deal with the divorces that are passed by the committee of the Senate at the present time.

subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
I have always stood up on my two feet and voted against any move to give more facilities for divorce. I have made my stand very clear since I have been in this house, and I have been here for seventeen years. I have always made my stand very clear on that. We do not believe in it because we say, and our Catholic faith says it, that to disrupt marriage is killing the union, is to a certain extent killing the children and killing the nation. That is what we believe.
I know that divorces are requested in the name of liberty and freedom because, as some people say, nobody will tell us what is evil and what is good. It has been said in this house and in various committees of the house-I was there to hear it-we cannot know what is evil and what is good. And when we say that divorce is evil they say: Who is going to tell us what is evil? Well, if disrupting the family, dividing the father and mother, separating them from their children is not evil, I do not know what evil is. No one is obliged to have a friend or a neighbour come and tell him that that is evil when speaking of divorce, disruption of the family, the killing of the nation and the separating of the children from their father and their mother. If that is not evil, well, words do not mean anything to me.
I am going to quote one of the Conservative members, a very able man, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). He was speaking in Montreal. I think I should quote this because it comes within the scope of my speech. He spoke on Monday, March 17, 1952. The article in the Gazette says in big type: "Real religious renaissance Diefenbaker cure for reds." That is a very good title because the communists of Russia have had experience of divorce, and they had to throw

it away. They had to go back on their philosophy, but only to a certain extent of course because they are atheists. But they had to come back and try to do something to prevent millions of children from wandering about the streets of Russia without a father and a mother to take care of them. The state had to do something for them. The burden became too heavy for the state, and they had to go back on their laws. They had to throw away some of their laws so as to render divorce more difficult in the future. It has been abundantly proven. The hon. member for Lake Centre called for a real religious renaissance. I think he should have added that this real religious renaissance should mean that we would think that it is a spiritual malady existing on our continent and on other continents of the globe. It is a spiritual malady to give more facilities and to admit the dissolubility of marriage on earth. I think he should be complimented on that because certainly he gave a lead so far as spiritual leadership is concerned in this country and in all countries of the world.
I remember that in 1950 the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke on this question and gave a very clear picture of what we of Quebec understood in respect to this matter. I believe the same bill was presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I should like to read that quotation of the Prime Minister, but before doing so I am going to give a few figures. I gave figures a few moments ago on divorce in the United States. From December 31, 1906, to December 31, 1916, there were 975,728 divorces in the United States. There were that many divorces in that ten-year period in the United States. From December 31, 1876, to December 31, 1916, there were 2,250,069 divorces in the United States. I have taken these figures from the "Voice of America". The "Voice of America" adds this, that the total number of persons separated in fifty years-and the word "separated" is absolutely accurate-was 4,500,138. The total number of minor children made orphans in fifty years-and, through divorces, they are really made orphans-was 1,689,662. Then the "Voice of America" makes this reference-and I ask hon. members to note the expression used- that the total number of persons bereft and dishonoured in fifty years was 6,189,800.
Those are strong words. I agree with them. Because I believe that if in this country we are going to follow the example of other countries in the matter of divorce, then in Canada we will have the condition that we see in other countries-a condition of national disaster.

We should be more careful. I see my hon. friend smiling. He has his opinions; I have mine. It is a national disaster to allow divorce, and to give more facilities for divorce.

No. This is what the Prime Minister said on June 20, 1950:
I do not intend to take very long, and I am not rising to talk this bill out, but to bring before the house certain facts . . . There is no doubt that under the British North America Act parliament has jurisdiction with respect to divorce. That is one of the express provisions of the act. There is also no doubt that before confederation there were in force in the province of Quebec laws which by virtue of the British North America Act continue in force until they are amended or repealed by the jurisdiction having authority to deal with them.
If we have authority to deal with them as suggested here, and if we give permission to those two provinces to go before the exchequer court, we are amending the law, whether we like it or not. Yes we are.

subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
The Prime Minister continued:
That is to be found in the explicit terms of section 129 of the British North America Act. Among the laws which were in force in the province of Quebec, and which have not been dealt with by the legislature of Quebec or by this parliament up to the present time, and which continue to be in force, is section 185 of the Quebec civil code. That is in force in the province of Quebec, and it is not in force anywhere else, and any legislation to deal with it is legislation for the province of Quebec and for the province of Quebec alone.

Divorce Jurisdiction
If the hon. member insists upon parliament accepting his bill, then he is asking parliament to overlook section 185 of the Quebec civil code. It would no longer be applicable in that province, because the hon. member would be saying to the people of Quebec, "You now have a divorce court known as the exchequer court. You are now allowed to go there, and with greater facilities available." It has been proven, and I say I have proven tonight conclusively from the quotations I have read, statements by political men in England, the United States and Canada, that in establishing divorce courts greater facility is given.
If that is done in the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland, then more facility is offered to those provinces. Section 185 of the Quebec civil code would no longer be applicable. The hon. member would be saying to the people of Quebec, "This law of yours is no longer applicable. You are now allowed to go before the exchequer court, and to obtain divorces as often as you wish." That is what my friend's bill is doing.
We do not want that. The Prime Minister had this to say:
That section of the code is very clear, and I think the shortest way to bring its content before hon. members is to read it. It is as follows:
"Marriage can only be dissolved by the natural death of one of the parties; while both live, it is indissoluble."
We believe that in Quebec.

speechtext: And the Senate overrides that section 300 times a year.

The question of whether the Senate is or is not a divorce court was established long ago. It is a special provision that has been acceptedbut not by and for the Catholics, because we are against it. We are against it. Then the Prime Minister continued:
Such is the Quebec law at the present time, and until that law is amended or repealed, the matter is not one of who will have jurisdiction to hear a divorce case; the matter to be dealt with consists of a fundamental declaration of the law and that is why the hon. members who introduced this bill took the precaution to declare that the exchequer court would have jurisdiction and would have the right to dissolve a marriage. That however would be legislating for the province of Quebec.
I suggest the authority of a statement by the Prime Minister is much better than anything I could say. He is speaking; I am only quoting him. I believe he is right, because he knows what he is talking about. Again quoting the Prime Minister:
That however would be legislating for the province of Quebec. It would be within the power of this parliament, but still it would be legislating on a matter which is extremely distasteful to the large majority of the people of that province.
He is telling my hon. friend, through my mouth, that it is distasteful to our province.
